**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 69, verses 1–3:**

﴿Al-Haqqah﴾ ﴿What is al-Haqqah?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what al-Haqqah is?﴾

*Al-Haqqah* is the form *fa'ilah* from *haqqa al-shay'* (the thing was established), meaning that its occurrence is confirmed. The *ha'* in it can only be one of two things:

[p. 112]

either a feminine marker (*ha' al-ta'nith*), in which case *al-Haqqah* is a qualifier of an implied feminine noun, or a verbal-noun marker in the pattern *fa'ilah*, like *al-kadhibah* for *al-kadhib* (lying), *al-khatimah* for *al-khatm* (sealing), *al-baqiyah* for *al-baqa'* (remaining), *al-taghiyah* for *al-tughyan* (rebellion), *al-nafilah*, and *al-khati'ah*. Its origin is the *ta'* of the single occurrence (*ta' al-marrah*), but when the verbal noun is intended, the notion of "single occurrence" is set aside, as with many verbal nouns of the pattern *fa'lah* that do not mean a single occurrence, such as the expression *darbah lazib* (a sticky clay, lit. "a clinging stroke"). Thus *al-Haqqah* means *al-haqq* (the truth), as one says *min haqq kadha* (from the truth of such-and-such), i.e., from its truth.

On both readings, *al-Haqqah* may mean the descriptive sense: an event that is bound to happen (*tahiqqu*), or a truth that is bound to come about (*yahiqqu*).

It may also be intended as a proper name (*laqab*) for the Day of Resurrection. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and his companions, and it is what the exegetes (*mufassirun*) generally adopted. The Day of Resurrection is so named because its occurrence is certain, as God says: ﴿and to warn of the Day of Gathering, about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. Or it is so named because rights are established on that Day, and reward for them is not lost. God says: ﴿and you will not be wronged even by a thread﴾ [al-Nisa': 77], and He says: ﴿so whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7], ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 8]. The choice of this root and this form allows many meanings suitable to this context to be included, and this is a wonderful brevity (*ijaz*), so that the minds of the listeners may go in every possible direction of terror and fear, by what its arrival is bound to bring upon them.

It is also possible that *al-Haqqah* is a qualifier of an implied noun, whose supposed form is *al-sa'ah al-haqqah* (the Hour that is bound to come) or *al-waqi'ah al-haqqah* (the event that is bound to come). In that case it is a threat of a Day or an event in which severe punishment will fall upon those who are warned, like the Day of Badr or its battle, and that this is a truth about which there is no doubt. Or it is a qualifier of the word (*kalimah*), meaning the word of God that became binding upon the polytheists of Makkah. God says: ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who disbelieved, that they are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 6]. Or it refers to the word that became binding for the Prophet (ﷺ) that God would give him victory. God says: ﴿And We have already given Our word to Our servants, the messengers, that they will surely be helped, and that Our soldiers will surely be the victors﴾ [al-Saffat: 171–173], ﴿so turn away from them for a time﴾ [al-Saffat: 174].

It may also be a verbal noun with the meaning of *al-haqq* (truth). It is then correct for it to qualify the Day of Resurrection, that it is true, as in His saying: ﴿and the true promise draws near﴾ [al-Anbiya': 97], or to qualify the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ [Al 'Imran: 62]. Or it may mean the whole truth that the Qur'an brought. God says:

[p. 113]

﴿This is Our Book, which speaks against you with truth﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29], and He says: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30].

The opening of the surah with this word is a means of striking awe into the polytheists.

*Al-Haqqah* is a *mubtada'* (subject), and *ma* is a second *mubtada'*. The *al-Haqqah* mentioned a second time is the *khabar* (predicate) of the second *mubtada'*, and the sentence formed by the second *mubtada'* and its predicate is the *khabar* of the first *mubtada'*.

*Ma* is an interrogative (*ism istifham*) used for emphasis and magnification (*tahwil wa ta'zim*), as if it were said: "Do you know what al-Haqqah is?", that is, "What is al-Haqqah?", meaning "al-Haqqah is a great thing." Repeating the subject's noun in the sentence that serves as its predicate takes the place of a pronoun in linking the sentence to its subject. This is the use of the noun in place of the pronoun (*al-idhar fi maqam al-idmar*) for the sake of the awe contained in the noun. A parallel for this is His saying: ﴿and the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 27].

The clause ﴿And what will make you know what al-Haqqah is?﴾ may be parenthetical (*mu'taridah*) between the clause ﴿What is al-Haqqah?﴾ and the clause ﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Haqqah: 4], and the *waw* is a parenthetical *waw*.

It is also possible that the clause is conjoined (*ma'tufah*) to the clause ﴿What is al-Haqqah?﴾.

The second *ma* is interrogative, and the interrogation through it is a figurative expression (*kinayah*) for the impossibility of human knowledge encompassing the reality (*kunh*) of al-Haqqah, because a thing that lies outside the familiar limit cannot easily be imagined, so it is natural to ask about its meaning.

The address in His saying ﴿And what will make you know﴾ is to an unspecified person. The meaning is: al-Haqqah is a great matter whose reality you cannot grasp.

The construction *ma adraka kadha* (what will make you know such-and-such) has become like a proverb (*mimma jara majra al-mathal*), so it is not changed from this wording. It is a compound construction made of the interrogative *ma* and the verb *adra*, which is transitive through the causative *hamzah* to three objects, in the pattern of *a'lama* and *ara*. Thus the subject of its base verb *dara* becomes the first object by means of the causative. The verb *adraka* has been suspended (*mu'allaq*) from governing two objects by the second interrogative *ma* in His saying ﴿What is al-Haqqah?﴾. The original sentence before the construction with the interrogative would be: "I knew al-Haqqah to be a great matter," and then it became: "So-and-so made me know al-Haqqah to be a great matter."

The first *ma* is interrogative, used for emphasis and magnification by way of metonymy (*majaz mursal*)

[p. 114]

in the particle, because a great matter is something about which one naturally asks, so magnification and interrogation become mutually implicated. You may also take the interrogation to be a denial (*istifham inkari*), meaning that no one knows the reality of this matter.

The intended meaning in both considerations is emphasis (*tahwil*).

This question is like when you say: "I know whether so-and-so will travel."

The third *ma* suspended the verb *adraka* from governing two objects.

The *kaf* of address in it is an address to an unspecified person, so it is not accompanied by a dual, plural, or feminine pronoun when addressed to someone other than a single masculine person.

The use of *ma adraka* differs from the use of *ma yudrika* in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63], and His saying: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17] in Surah al-Shura.

It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "Everything in the Qur'an that comes after *ma adraka* has been made known to him, and everything that comes after *wa ma yudrika* has been concealed from him." This was also reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah and from Yahya ibn Sallam. If this report is authentic, its meaning is that the object of *ma adraka* is certain to occur, because the interrogation in it is for emphasis, while the object of *ma yudrika* is not certain to occur, because the interrogation in it is a denial, which amounts to negating knowledge.

Al-Raghib said: "Every place in the Qur'an where *wa ma adraka* is mentioned is followed by its explanation, such as: ﴿And what will make you know what it is? A blazing fire﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 10], ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is? The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 2–3], ﴿Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is? Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is? A Day on which no soul can do anything for another﴾ [al-Infitar: 18–19], ﴿And what will make you know what al-Haqqah is? Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3–4]." It seems he intended to explain what was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

I have not seen any of the linguists who gave this construction its due in explanation, and some of them did not mention it at all.

A Day on which no soul can do anything for another﴾ [al-Infitar: 18–19], ﴿And what will make you know what al-Haqqah is? Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3–4]." It seems he intended to explain what was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

I have not seen any of the linguists who gave this construction its due in explanation, and some of them did not mention it at all.

[Page 115]

﴿Thamūd and ʿĀd denied the Striking Calamity.﴾ If you take His saying ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 3] as the end of a speech, then the position of His saying

[Page 115 continued]

﴿Thamūd and ʿĀd denied the Striking Calamity﴾ and what is connected to it is a resumptive new sentence (istiʾnāf). It is a reminder of what befell Thamūd and ʿĀd because they denied resurrection and recompense, and an allusion to the polytheists of Makkah, warning them that there may befall them the like of what befell Thamūd and ʿĀd, since they are equal in denying resurrection. On this reading, His saying "the Inevitable Reality" and so on serves as a preparation (tawṭiʾah) and a paving (tamhīd) for this great admonition, to strike awe into the hearts of the listeners.

If you take the speech as connected to the clause ﴿Thamūd and ʿĀd denied the Striking Calamity﴾, and you specify the term "the Inevitable Reality" as referring to the Day of Resurrection, then this clause is a third predicate (khabar thālith) about "the Inevitable Reality."

The meaning is: Thamūd and ʿĀd denied it (the Inevitable Reality). According to the apparent construction, it should have been expressed with a pronoun referring to "the Inevitable Reality," so one would say: "Thamūd and ʿĀd denied it." Instead, the speech turns to the explicit naming of "the Striking Calamity," because "the Striking Calamity" is synonymous with "the Inevitable Reality" in one of the two senses the term "the Inevitable Reality" may bear. This serves as an elucidation of the awesomeness expressed in His saying ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 3].

What is meant by "the Striking Calamity" is what is meant by "the Inevitable Reality."

Thamūd and ʿĀd are mentioned first among the denying nations because they are the most widely known denying nations among the polytheists of Makkah, since they are of the Arab peoples, and because their dwellings are adjacent, one to the north and the other to the south.

Al-qāriʿah (the Striking Calamity) is an active participle (ism fāʿil) from qaraʿahu, meaning he struck him with a strong blow. It is said: qaraʿa al-baʿīr (he struck the camel). And it is said: "The slave is struck with the stick." Admonitions by which the soul is broken are called qawāriʿ (striking things), because of the restraint they impose on people from deeds. In the first maqāmah (assembly narrative) it says: "and he strikes the ears with the rebukes of his admonition." Reproach is called taqrīʿ, and in the proverb: "The stick is not struck for him, and the pebbles are not shaken for him." Its origin is in ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarib al-ʿAdwānī, in a story to which al-Mutalammis alluded in a verse.

Here, al-qāriʿah is an attribute of an omitted noun, whose wording is estimated as feminine so as to agree with its mentioned attribute, such as al-sāʿah (the Hour) or al-qiyāmah (the Resurrection). "Al-qāriʿah" means: that which strikes people with terrors and frights; or that which strikes existing things with a striking, like the crumbling of the mountains, the sinking of the earth, the obliterating of the stars, and the eclipse of the sun in an eclipse that has no clearing, so that this is likened to striking.

The description of the Hour or the Resurrection with this attribute is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), in which the attribute is ascribed to something other than what it truly belongs to, by an interpretation based on its association with what it truly belongs to, since it is the time of striking. God, exalted is He, said:

[Page 116]

﴿The Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Qāriʿah: 1], ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qāriʿah: 2], ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [al-Qāriʿah: 3], ﴿A Day when people will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qāriʿah: 4], to the end of the verse. Its explanation will come in His saying ﴿And when the Horn is blown with one blast﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 13], and the verses following.

In the report about these two nations, the rhetorical device of wrapping and unfolding (lafф wa nashr) is employed, because the two of them shared in the cause of punishment; then the mention of their punishment is detailed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verse 5:

﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming (al-Taghiyah)﴾ He began with the mention of Thamud because the punishment that befell them was of the kind of the thunderbolt, since the thunderbolts struck them, which are called in some verses "the Cry" (al-Sayhah). And al-Taghiyah: it is the thunderbolt, according to the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah: a thunderbolt or thunderbolts descended upon them and destroyed them. Also, the dwellings of Thamud were on the route of the people of Makkah to al-Sham on their journeys, so they would see them. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿So those are their dwellings, empty (khawiyah) because of what they did wrong﴾ [al-Naml: 52]. Also, the discourse on the destruction of 'Ad is more fitting, so Thamud was placed later for this reason as well.

The thunderbolt or the Cry was named al-Taghiyah because it exceeded the familiar degree of severity, so its action was likened to the action of the tyrant (al-Taghi), who exceeds the limit in aggression and violence.

The letter ba' in the phrase "bi-al-Taghiyah" (by the overwhelming) denotes instrumentality (li-al-isti'anah).

Thamud: a people of the extinct, original Arabs (al-'Arabah al-ba'idah al-'aribah), and they are the lineage of 'Ad. Thamud is the name of the forefather of that people, but it came to dominate the people, and therefore it is diptote (mamnu' min al-sarf) due to being a proper noun (al-'alamiyyah) and feminine gender (al-ta'nith), considering it as a people or tribe.

The mention of Thamud has already occurred at the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih﴾ [al-A'raf: 73] in Surah al-A'raf.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 69, verses 6–7**

﴿As for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a furious, roaring wind﴾ ﴿which He unleashed against them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so that you would see the people lying prostrate in it as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees﴾.

*al-Ṣarṣar* is the violent wind that produces a sound like a screech. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during inauspicious days﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 16], in the Sūrah of Fuṣṣilat. *Al-ʿĀtiyah* is the wind of intense force. The root meaning of *ʿutuww* and *ʿutiyy* is extreme arrogance. The word was used as a metaphor for anything that exceeds the familiar limit, by analogy with intense arrogance in disobeying and departing from what is customary.

[Page 117]

*Al-taskhīr* means compelling someone to a task. It is used here as a metaphor for the formation of the roaring wind in a way that exceeds what is customary in the strength of its kind, as though it were forced into that act.

The phrase *ʿalayhim* ("against them") is governed by the verb, because it is treated as implying the meaning of *arsalahā* ("sent it").

*Ḥusūman* may be the plural of *ḥāsim*, like *quʿūd* as the plural of *qāʿid* and *shuhūd* as the plural of *shāhid*. In that case the masculine plural is given precedence for the days over the nights, because the days are more numerous, since they are eight. This word has several meanings:

First, it may mean that each part follows the others without a break, as in the expression *ṣiyām shahrayn mutatābiʿayn* ("fasting two consecutive months"). ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Zurārah al-Kilābī said:

*So a time came between them in which years followed one another without end (ḥusūm).*

It is said that *ḥusūm* derives from *ḥasm al-dāʾ bi-l-mikwāh* ("cauterising a disease with a branding iron"), since the cauterising is repeated over days. Its use here would then be a metaphor. This may be one of the innovations of the Qur'an, and the verse of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Kilābī belongs to Islamic-era poetry, so it follows the usage of the Qur'an.

The second meaning: it derives from *ḥasm*, which means cutting off, so that the wind is decisive and uprooting. From this the sword is called *ḥusām*, because it cuts. The meaning is that it destroyed them and left none of them. On both of these meanings, *ḥusūman* is an adjective of *sabʿa layālin wa thamāniyata ayyām* ("seven nights and eight days"), or a circumstantial qualifier of them.

The third meaning: *ḥusūm* is a verbal noun like *shukūr* and *dukhūl*, and so it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*), and its governing verb is *sakhkharahā* ("He unleashed it"). The meaning is that He unleashed it against them in order to annihilate them and cut off their remnant.

All these meanings are suitable to be attached to these days, so the choice of this word is part of the full eloquence and inimitability (*iʿjāz*) of the Qur'an.

Some Muslim astronomers and calendar-keepers (*aṣḥāb al-mīqāt*) named eight days, roughly between the end of February and the beginning of March, which are known in the customary pattern of the weather for strong winds. They called them the "days of *ḥusūm*" as a comparison. They claimed that these days correspond to the same days of the year in which ʿĀd was struck by the winds. This is among the illusions, and who has observed those days?

Some philologists claimed that the days of *ḥusūm* are the days called "days of the old woman" (*ayyām al-ʿajūz*) or "days of the *ʿajz*", which are the last part of winter. The Arabs counted them as five or seven, and they have known names gathered in verses mentioned in the books of philology. Yet how far they are from the *ḥusūm* of ʿĀd, in number and duration!

From His saying ﴿He unleashed it against them﴾ follows that they all became prostrate, so that anyone who witnessed that state, had he been present, would see them.

The address in His saying *fa-tarā* ("so you see") is addressed to an unspecified person, that is, "whoever sees, if he were a viewer." This is a style used in narrating great events that are absent, in which that state is brought to mind as though it were present. In that setting one imagines a present listener who witnessed their destruction or witnessed them after it. Both kinds of witnessing are absent in this verse, so it is considered a supposed address (*khiṭāb farḍī*). It is therefore not an *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical person), nor is it an address to an unspecified person. Similar to it is His saying, ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled by disgrace﴾ [al-Shūrā: 45], and His saying, ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom﴾ [al-Insān: 20]. Because of the subtlety of this usage, the exegetes neglected to address it, except for one word from al-Bayḍāwī.

The definite article in *al-qawm* ("the people") is for a known referent that has been mentioned (*al-ʿahd al-dhikrī*). *Al-qawm* means the tribe, and this is a depiction of the destruction of the entire tribe.

The pronoun in *fīhā* ("in it") refers back to the nights and the days.

*Ṣarʿā* is the plural of *ṣarīʿ*, meaning one who has fallen to the ground dead. They were compared to *aʿjāz nakhl*, that is, the trunks of palm trees. The *ʿajz* of a palm tree is the stem that joins the palm to the ground; it is the thickest and firmest part of the palm.

The point of comparison with it is that when people cut down palm trees to benefit from their timber in building houses, for roofs and door-frames, they select the trunks, because they are thicker and fuller, and they leave them on the ground until they dry out and their moisture departs. Then they make them into pillars and columns.

*Al-nakhl* is a collective noun whose singular is *nakhlah*.

*Al-khāwī* means one emptied of what used to fill it and inhabit it.

[Page 119]

The word *khāwiyah* ("hollow") in His saying is in the genitive case by the unanimous agreement of the readers (*qurrāʾ*), so it must be an adjective of *nakhl*.

The description of *nakhl* as *khāwiyah* is based on the application of the name "palm" to its place, by interpreting it as a garden or an orchard. Thus there is a figure of speech called *istikhdām* (a word used in two senses). The meaning is: empty of people. This description serves to disfigure the thing compared, by disfiguring its place. It has no effect on the resemblance itself, but the best of such description is that which is suited to the purpose of the comparison, as in this verse, where this description has a striking effect in repelling them from their state, so as to fit the admonition and the warning against falling into the like of their causes.

From this is the saying of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

*That is more awe-inspiring to me when I speak to him, though it is said that you are a man of lineage who is questioned.*

*From a lion, among the lions of the lions, whose den is the lairs of the valley, a thicket behind which lies another thicket.* (The four lines.)

And the saying of ʿAntarah:

*I left him to the beasts of prey, which gnaw at him, eating the beauty of his fingers and wrist.*

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verse 8:

﴿Then do you see any remnant of them?﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') drawn from the two stories of Thamud and 'Ad together. It is a summary (fadhlaka) of what was detailed about the manner of their destruction. This is of the type of "combining after separating," so the verse contains a combining, then a separating, then a combining again. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50] ﴿and Thamud, and spared none﴾ [al-Najm: 51]. That is, He did not spare either of them.

The address is to an unspecified person.

The word "baqiyah" (remnant) may be an active participle (ism fa'il) in its original sense, and the "ha'" is either for the feminine, with the interpretation of "soul" (nafs), meaning "then no soul of them is seen remaining," or with the interpretation of "group" (firqah), meaning "no group of them is seen remaining."

It is also possible that "baqiyah" is a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern of "fa'ilah," like what preceded in al-Haqqah, meaning "then you do not see for them any survival," that is, they perished to the last one.

The "lam" in His saying "for them" (lahum) may be taken to denote a kind of ownership, meaning "remaining for the sake of benefit." It may also be that the "lam" has the meaning of "min" (from), as in the expression "I heard a cry from him" (sami'tu lahu sarakhan), and the saying of al-A'sha:

Page 120

We hear from the jewelry a rustling whenever she turns, as the stalk of the reed (?) makes a sound when the wind passes through it.

And the saying of Jarir:

"And we, from among you, are better on the Day of Resurrection."
That is, "and we are better than you."

It is also possible that the "lam" is the one that is understood in the construction of the annexation (idafah), when the annexation is not in the sense of "min." The original form is: "then do you see their remnant?" When the intent was to make explicit the generality of the negation, and that required bringing in the superfluous "min," the noun following the superfluous "min" had to be indefinite. So the sense of the annexation was given its due by manifesting the "lam" that is normally understood, as in His saying: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾ [al-Isra': 5], for its original form is "servants of Us."

The prepositional phrase introduced by "lam" stands in the position of a qualifier (na't) of "baqiyah," but it was placed before it, so it became a circumstantial (hal).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 9–10:

﴿And Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities with sin.﴾ ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, and He seized them with a seizing overwhelming.﴾ It is coordinated with the clause ﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity.﴾ [al-Haqqah: 4].

In this mention, several nations that preceded the sending of Musa (peace be upon him) are gathered together, both in general and by explicit naming. Among them, the ones singled out explicitly are the people of Pharaoh and the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikat), because they are among the most widely mentioned nations among the People of the Book who mixed with the Arabs and lived in their neighborhood, so some Arabs would reach some of the news of their story.

In coordinating these with Thamud and 'Ad within the context of mentioning denial of the Striking Calamity, there is a hint that they resembled one another in denying the Striking Calamity, just as they resembled one another in coming with the sin (al-khati'ah) and in disobeying the messengers of their Lord. Thus there occurs in the speech what is called ihtibak (a rhetorical interweaving in which each part omits what the other mentions).

By Pharaoh is meant the Pharaoh to whom Musa (peace be upon him) was sent, and he is Minephtah the Second. The sin is attributed to him because Musa was sent to him to release the Children of Israel from bondage. God the Exalted said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24]. So he is the one held responsible for this disobedience, and the Copts followed him in obedience to his command, denied Musa, and turned away from his call.

His saying ﴿and those before him﴾ includes many nations, among them the people of Nuh and the people of Ibrahim.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa man qablahu﴾ with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the ba'. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning "and those who were from his side," i.e., his people and followers.

Al-Mu'tafikat: the three cities of the people of Lut, and by al-Mu'tafikat is meant their inhabitants, namely the people of Lut. They are singled out for mention because of the notoriety of their crime, and because they were well known among the Arabs, since their towns were on their route to al-Sham. God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning﴾ [al-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 138], and He said: ﴿And they have certainly passed by the city upon which was rained a rain of evil. Have they not been seeing it?﴾ [al-Furqan: 40].

The towns of the people of Lut are described as al-Mu'tafikat, the plural of mu'tafikah, an active participle of i'tafaka, the intransitive form of afakahu, meaning when he overturns it. So they are "the overturned ones," i.e., the one who overturned them (the Creator) turned them over, meaning He caused them to sink. God the Exalted said: ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest﴾ [al-Hijr: 74].

Al-Khati'ah: it is either a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern fa'ilah, whose ta' marks a single instance; but since it is used as a verbal noun, the notion of a single instance is disregarded, as already explained at His saying (al-Haqqah). It is then a masdar of khati'a, meaning he sinned. The sin is khit' (with a kasra on the kha'). Or it is an active participle of khati'a with its feminine form, interpreted as "the sinful deed possessing sin," in which case its ha' is the feminine ha'.

The definite article in it is the definite article of the genus under both interpretations, so the meaning is: each of them came with the sin that deserves punishment. Following from this is the detailed explanation of their sin, expressed by al-khati'ah, when He said ﴿so they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾. This subsequent elaboration is of the same type as the subsequent elaboration in His saying ﴿The people of Nuh denied before them; they denied Our servant and said, "A madman," and he was rebuked﴾ [al-Qamar: 9], in that it is an explanatory elaboration following what was made general.

The pronoun in 'asaw (they disobeyed) may refer to Pharaoh in his capacity as the head of his people, so the pronoun refers to him and to his people. The indication is clear according to the reading of al-Jumhur; and as for the reading of Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i, the matter is more evident. On this consideration, the referent of the pronoun in 'asaw is the messenger of their Lord, meaning Musa (peace be upon him). Its definiteness through the idafah (construct) indicates their error in worshipping Pharaoh and making him their god.

It is also permissible that the pronoun in 'asaw refers to ﴿Pharaoh and those before him and the overturned cities﴾.

﴿The messenger of their Lord﴾ is the messenger sent to each of these peoples.

The singular "rasul" here is meant distributively across the groups, i.e., a messenger of God for each group among them; the indication is clear. This is more elegant in arrangement than saying "fa'asaw rusula rabbihim," because the singular "rasul" carries a variation in forms of words between plural and singular, avoiding the succession of three plurals; the plural forms are not free from heaviness due to their infrequent use. The opposite is His saying in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿And the people of Nuh, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37], although they denied only one messenger; and His saying ﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105] and what follows it in Surat al-Shu'ara. The interpretation of this has already been given in its place.

Al-akhdh (the seizing) is used in the sense of destruction, as has already been explained at His saying ﴿We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44] in Surat al-An'am and in other places.

And "akhdhatan" is a single instance of the seizing; so it means the seizing of Pharaoh and his people by drowning, as God the Exalted said: ﴿So We seized them, the seizing of one Mighty, Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 42]. And if the third-person pronoun is returned to ﴿Pharaoh and those before him and the overturned cities﴾, then the singular "akhdhatan" is like the singular "rasul rabbihim," meaning We seized each nation of them with a seizing.

Al-rabiyah: an active participle from raba, yarbu, meaning it increased. When it was formed into the pattern fa'ilah, the waw was changed to ya' because it fell in a moving position after a kasra.

Rubuw is used here metaphorically for intensity, just as abundance is used metaphorically for intensity in such as His saying ﴿and call out today for one destruction, but call for destruction many times﴾ [al-Furqan: 14].

And what is meant by the overwhelming seizing (al-akhdhah al-rabiyah) is the destruction of extermination, i.e., there was no remnant left among them in their destruction.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 9–10:

﴿And Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities with sin.﴾ ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, and He seized them with a seizing overwhelming.﴾ It is coordinated with the clause ﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity.﴾ [al-Haqqah: 4].

In this mention, several nations that preceded the sending of Musa (peace be upon him) are gathered together, both in general and by explicit naming. Among them, the ones singled out explicitly are the people of Pharaoh and the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikat), because they are among the most widely mentioned nations among the People of the Book who mixed with the Arabs and lived in their neighborhood, so some Arabs would reach some of the news of their story.

In coordinating these with Thamud and 'Ad within the context of mentioning denial of the Striking Calamity, there is a hint that they resembled one another in denying the Striking Calamity, just as they resembled one another in coming with the sin (al-khati'ah) and in disobeying the messengers of their Lord. Thus there occurs in the speech what is called ihtibak (a rhetorical interweaving in which each part omits what the other mentions).

By Pharaoh is meant the Pharaoh to whom Musa (peace be upon him) was sent, and he is Minephtah the Second. The sin is attributed to him because Musa was sent to him to release the Children of Israel from bondage. God the Exalted said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24]. So he is the one held responsible for this disobedience, and the Copts followed him in obedience to his command, denied Musa, and turned away from his call.

His saying ﴿and those before him﴾ includes many nations, among them the people of Nuh and the people of Ibrahim.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa man qablahu﴾ with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the ba'. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning "and those who were from his side," i.e., his people and followers.

Al-Mu'tafikat: the three cities of the people of Lut, and by al-Mu'tafikat is meant their inhabitants, namely the people of Lut. They are singled out for mention because of the notoriety of their crime, and because they were well known among the Arabs, since their towns were on their route to al-Sham. God the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning﴾ [al-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 138], and He said: ﴿And they have certainly passed by the city upon which was rained a rain of evil. Have they not been seeing it?﴾ [al-Furqan: 40].

The towns of the people of Lut are described as al-Mu'tafikat, the plural of mu'tafikah, an active participle of i'tafaka, the intransitive form of afakahu, meaning when he overturns it. So they are "the overturned ones," i.e., the one who overturned them (the Creator) turned them over, meaning He caused them to sink. God the Exalted said: ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest﴾ [al-Hijr: 74].

Al-Khati'ah: it is either a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern fa'ilah, whose ta' marks a single instance; but since it is used as a verbal noun, the notion of a single instance is disregarded, as already explained at His saying (al-Haqqah). It is then a masdar of khati'a, meaning he sinned. The sin is khit' (with a kasra on the kha'). Or it is an active participle of khati'a with its feminine form, interpreted as "the sinful deed possessing sin," in which case its ha' is the feminine ha'.

The definite article in it is the definite article of the genus under both interpretations, so the meaning is: each of them came with the sin that deserves punishment. Following from this is the detailed explanation of their sin, expressed by al-khati'ah, when He said ﴿so they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾. This subsequent elaboration is of the same type as the subsequent elaboration in His saying ﴿The people of Nuh denied before them; they denied Our servant and said, "A madman," and he was rebuked﴾ [al-Qamar: 9], in that it is an explanatory elaboration following what was made general.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 11–12:

﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ ﴿so that We might make it a reminder for you, and that an attentive ear might retain it﴾. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and those before him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 9], since it encompasses the people of Nuh, who were the first of the nations to deny the messengers,

Page 123

made the abrupt mention of the reminder fitting, by taking into account what it contains of an incorporated favor (idmaj imtinan) upon all the people who descended from the group whom Allah saved from drowning. This is so that it may pass from being an admonition and a lesson to a reminder that it is a blessing; and this is of the category of incorporation (al-idmaj).

The destruction of the people of Nuh is well known, so it was treated as if it had been mentioned in the discourse, and so it was made the condition for (lamma) in His saying ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾, meaning: at that time, which is known for the overflowing of the flood.

Al-tughyan (overflowing): it is a metaphor for its extraordinary severity, which exceeds custom, likening it to the overbearing of a tyrant over people, a comparison made for approximation, for the flood is stronger in severity than the tyrant's oppression.

Al-jariyah (the sailing ship): it is an attribute of an omitted noun, which is the ship (al-safinah). This description became so common that it took the place of a proper noun. Allah, the Exalted, said (﴿And His are the ships rising high in the sea﴾ [al-Rahman: 24]).

The root meaning of carrying (al-haml) is placing one body upon another in order to transport it; here it is applied, by way of metaphor, to placing (people) within a moving vessel.

Attributing the carrying to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), based on the fact that He revealed to Nuh the building of the carrying vessel and the placing of the carried. Allah, the Exalted, said ﴿So We revealed to him: Build the ship under Our eyes and by Our revelation; then when Our command comes and the oven boils over, load into it of each kind two mates﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 27], and so on.

One of the wisdoms and causes of this carrying is mentioned: the wisdom of reminding mankind of it across the successive ages, so that it may be a motive for them to give thanks and an admonition to them against the evils of disbelief, and so that whoever knows it may inform those who have not known it, so that their ears may retain it.

By "an ear" is meant ears that retain. The generality of an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is not established except by an indicator of generalization, like His saying ﴿and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow﴾ [al-Hashr: 18].

Al-wa'y (retention): knowledge of what is heard, meaning: so that an ear described as retaining may know its report, i.e., one whose nature is to retain.

This is an allusion (ta'rid) against the polytheists, for they did not take heed of the report of the flood and of the ship in which the believers were saved, and so they received it as they receive humorous tales.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 13–18:

[p. 124]
﴿And when the Trumpet is blown with one blast﴾ ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing﴾ ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ ﴿and the sky will split, for on that Day it will be frail﴾ ﴿and the angels will be upon its edges; and above them, on that Day, eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ ﴿on that Day you will be exposed; not a secret of yours will be concealed﴾. The fa' (then) here serves to link what follows to the terror with which the surah opened, from His saying ﴿The Inevitable Reality﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1] ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 2] ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3]. So it is understood that this is a terrifying description of the punishment with which the polytheists were threatened, of the kind that befell their likes in this world, and of the punishment of the Hereafter that awaits them. When He had completed the threat of punishment in this world, He followed it with a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, which befalls at the Striking Calamity that they denied, just as Thamud and 'Ad denied it. Thus there is an explanation of the Striking Calamity: that it is the Hour of Resurrection, which is the Event that occurs.

As for al-sur (the Trumpet): it is a horn of a bull that is hollowed out, and inside it a plug is placed that fills part of its emptiness, so that when a blower blows into it, the air is compressed and it produces a strong sound. Armies used to employ it to call one another when they wished to mobilize or to attack. This was discussed earlier, at His saying, ﴿And His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-An'am: 73], in Surat al-An'am.

The blowing into the Trumpet (al-nafkh fi al-sur) is an expression for the command of bringing into being, by reviving bodies for the Resurrection, like the reviving by the call of a group of soldiers charged with the horns to summon the rest of the army, where no soldier delays from coming to the place of the call. It may also be that there is an existent angel assigned to it who produces a powerful sound.

As for nafkhah (a blast): it is a verbal noun of nafakha, joined with a ta' indicating the single occurrence, i.e. unity. It is in origin an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), or it may stand in the place of the agent, since it is known that the one who blows is the angel assigned to blow the Trumpet, who is Israfil.

The description of nafkhah as wahidah (one) is an emphasis, to convey unity from the form of fa'lah, explicitly confirming the unity conveyed by the ta'.

The specification of this is to draw attention to the marvel at the influence upon all human bodies

[p. 125]
by a single blast, without repetition, marvelling at the great power of God and the efficacy of His command. For the context of the speech from the beginning of the surah is the terrifying of the Day of Resurrection, so enumerating its terrors is the aim. For the sake of directing attention to this here, the description wahidah is not mentioned in His saying, ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command; then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come forth﴾ [al-Rum: 25], in Surat al-Rum.

Thus from the mention of ﴿one blast﴾ results the emphasis of the meaning of blowing and the emphasis of the meaning of unity. This clarifies what was transmitted from the author of al-Kashshaf in his explanation with a general wording, transmitted by al-Tibi. The intent of describing it as wahidah is not that it is not followed by a second, for it has come in other verses that there are two blasts. Rather, the intent is that it does not need its repetition for the purpose to be achieved, as a metaphor for the swiftness of the occurrence of the Event, i.e. the Day of the Event.

As for the mention of the word nafkhah, it is so that the description of unity can be applied to it. The mention of nafkhah is a follower, not the subject of the speech. So this blast is the first, which heralds the end of the world; then the second blast occurs, which will be at the resurrection of the dead.

The clause ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted﴾ etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because the crushing of the earth and the mountains may occur before the blowing into the Trumpet, since by it the world passes away.

The meaning of hummilat (lifted): they are removed from their places, by the earth with its mountains being moved away from its usual orbit, so that they collide with other bodies in space and are crushed. This condition is likened to a carrier carrying something in order to throw it onto the ground, like the carrying of a ball between players. It is also possible that the action of the angels charged with disrupting the order of the world, upon the terrestrial sphere, by moving it away from its orbit, is likened to carrying. All of this occurs when the gravitational force, which God made to preserve the order of the world, becomes disturbed, up to a term known to God, exalted is He.

Al-dakk: a severe striking that breaks the struck object, i.e. when the parts of the earth and the parts of its mountains are scattered.

The verbs nufikha, hummilat and dukkata are in the passive voice, because the purpose is connected to explaining the object rather than the agent. The agent of those actions is either the angels or what God has placed in them of causes of those actions, all by God's permission and power.

[p. 126]
The clause ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ contains the answer to idha ("when"), namely His saying ﴿the Inevitable Event will occur﴾. As for His saying "then on that Day," it is an emphasis of the meaning of ﴿when the Trumpet is blown﴾ etc., because the tanwin of yawma'idhin is a replacement for a clause indicated by the clause ﴿is blown in the Trumpet﴾ up to His saying ﴿one crushing﴾; that is, "the day when the Trumpet is blown, to its end, the Inevitable Event will occur." It is a verbal emphasis with a synonym of the emphasized term, for the meaning of yawm in His saying ﴿then on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ is absolute time, as is generally the case when it is in construct with idha.

The meaning of ﴿the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ is the realization of what was expected to occur, for they were being threatened with a great event; on that Day what they were threatened with will be realized.

So He expressed it with the past tense, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence.

The meaning: then at that time the Event will occur.

Al-waqi'ah is synonymous with al-haqqah and al-qari'ah, so mentioning it explicitly in place of a pronoun serves to increase the terror and to convey the conditions indicated by the derivational sources of the descriptions al-haqqah, al-qari'ah and al-waqi'ah.

Al-waqi'ah has become a proper name by predominance in the terminology of the Qur'an for the Day of Resurrection. God said, ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1] ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 2].

The verb ﴿the sky will split﴾ [al-Rahman: 37] may be coordinated with the clause ﴿is blown in the Trumpet﴾, so that it is attached to the condition of idha, and the postponement of its coordination is because of what is joined to this splitting: the description of the angels surrounding it, and the mention of the Throne that encompasses the heavens and mention of its bearers.

It may also be a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause, with the estimate: "and the sky has split."

The splitting of the sky is its being affected by the verb of splitting. Shaqq is the opening of passages in its surface. God said, ﴿And on the Day the sky is split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25] ﴿The dominion that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan: 26].

Then it is possible that this is other than the splitting in His saying ﴿So when the sky is split and becomes red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], and it is possible that it is that same one.

[p. 127]
The literal meaning of wahiyah is weak and scattered, and wahy is used metaphorically for ease and lack of resistance; one says, "his resolve weakened" when he becomes lenient and yielding. In the proverb: "Weaker than the spider's web," said of a case where proof does not stand.

Its restriction to yawma'idhin indicates that the weakening came upon it after it had been firm through the cohesion of its parts, which is what the Qur'an expresses as ratq (joined), just as it expresses splitting as fatq (unjoining). That is, on that day it is opened and passable.

Wahy is close to wahn (weakness). Most often wahy is applied to non-rational things, and wahn is applied to people.

The meaning: the angels move back and forth through it, ascending and descending, contrary to its former condition. God said, ﴿So when the sky is split and becomes red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

The clause ﴿and the angel is upon its edges﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in fahiya; that is, on that day the angel is upon its edges.

Al-malak: its root meaning is one of the angels, and its definiteness here is the definiteness of the genus, and it carries the sense of plurality, i.e. the genus of angel, meaning a group of angels or all the angels if comprehensiveness is intended. The comprehensive sense of a singular noun is more explicit in indicating totality. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said, "al-Kitab is more than the books," and from it is His saying, ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened﴾ [Maryam: 4].

The pronoun in arja'iha refers to the sky.

The meaning: the angels work in the regions of the sky, carrying out the descent of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the driving of the people of Hellfire into the Fire.

ʿArsh al-Rabb: a name for what encompasses the heavens, and it is greater than the heavens.

By the eight who carry the Throne are meant eight of the angels. It was said: eight persons; it was said: eight rows; it was said: eight tenths, i.e. about eighty out of the total number of angels; and other things were said. This is among the unseen matters whose details are not the purpose,

[p. 128]
since the aim of the verse is to depict the greatness of God, exalted is He, and to bring that closer to understanding, as He said in other verses.

Perhaps the purpose of the allusion to what exceeds the admonition is that God taught His Prophet ﷺ some of those conditions by a symbolic method, through which understanding of their details is opened to him, and He did not intend to occupy us with knowledge of them.

It seems that the motive for mentioning them in summary is the transition to reporting about the Throne of God, so that its mention would not be abrupt after the mention of the angels.

al-Tirmidhi transmitted from al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, from the Prophet ﷺ, a hadith in which he mentioned the distances between the heavens. In the mention of the phrase "the Throne" there are symbols that al-Tirmidhi cited in the manner of an explanation of this verse. One of its narrators is 'Abdullah ibn 'Umayrah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays. al-Bukhari said: "We do not know that he heard from al-Ahnaf."

There are other reports besides the hadith of al-'Abbas that are not regarded. Ibn al-'Arabi said concerning them: they are fabrications from the People of the Book, or from the poetry of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, and it is not established that the Prophet ﷺ had it recited before him and affirmed it. End.

The pronoun in fawqahum refers to the angel.

fawqahum is connected to ﴿bears the Throne of your Lord﴾ and it is an emphasis of what the verb "bears" indicates of the Throne being elevated; it is thus in the position of the two restrictions in His saying, ﴿There is no creature on the earth nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ. The attribution of "Throne" to God is an attribution of honour, like the attribution of the Ka'bah to Him in His saying, ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], and God is exalted above sitting on the Throne and above dwelling in a house.

The address in His saying ("you will be exposed") is to all people, by the indication of the context and what follows of detail.

Al-'ard (exposition): its root meaning is passing things before one who wishes to examine them, like presenting merchandise to a buyer or reviewing an army before its commander. It is used here metaphorically for its necessary consequence, which is reckoning, while the literal meaning remains permissible.

[p. 129]
The meaning of ﴿not a secret of yours will be concealed﴾: nothing will be hidden from God or from His angels. The feminine form of khafiyah is because it is an adjective for a feminine noun understood either as an act of the servants, estimated as "a deed," or as "a soul," i.e. no soul's secret will be hidden from the reckoning, and no sinner will be confused with a believer, nor a righteous person with a wicked one.

The clause ﴿on that Day you will be exposed﴾ is a new sentence, or it is an explanation of the clause ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾, or it is a substitution of inclusion from it.

"Minkum" (of you) is a description of khafiyah, placed before it, so it is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

[p. 124]

So it is understood that this is a terrifying description of the punishment with which the polytheists were threatened, of the kind that befell their likes in this world, and of the punishment of the Hereafter that awaits them. Thus there is an explanation of the Striking Calamity: that it is the Hour of Resurrection, which is the Event that occurs.

The specification of this is to draw attention to the marvel at the influence upon all human bodies

[p. 125]

Rather, the intent is that it does not need its repetition for the purpose to be achieved, as a metaphor for the swiftness of the occurrence of the Event, i.e. the Day of the Event.

As for the mention of the word nafkhah, it is so that the description of unity can be applied to it. The mention of nafkhah is a follower, not the subject of the speech. So this blast is the first, which heralds the end of the world; then the second blast occurs, which will be at the resurrection of the dead.

The meaning of hummilat (lifted): they are removed from their places, by the earth with its mountains being moved away from its usual orbit, so that they collide with other bodies in space and are crushed. This condition is likened to a carrier carrying something in order to throw it onto the ground, like the carrying of a ball between players. It is also possible that the action of the angels charged with disrupting the order of the world, upon the terrestrial sphere, by moving it away from its orbit, is likened to carrying. All of this occurs when the gravitational force, which God made to preserve the order of the world, becomes disturbed, up to a term known to God, exalted is He.

Al-dakk: a severe striking that breaks the struck object, i.e. when the parts of the earth and the parts of its mountains are scattered.

The verbs nufikha, hummilat and dukkata are in the passive voice, because the purpose is connected to explaining the object rather than the agent. The agent of those actions is either the angels or what God has placed in them of causes of those actions, all by God's permission and power.

[p. 126]

[p. 127]

The meaning: the angels move back and forth through it, ascending and descending, contrary to its former condition. God said, ﴿So when the sky is split and becomes red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

The pronoun in arja'iha refers to the sky.

The meaning: the angels work in the regions of the sky, carrying out the descent of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the driving of the people of Hellfire into the Fire.

ʿArsh al-Rabb: a name for what encompasses the heavens, and it is greater than the heavens.

End.

﴿And when the Trumpet is blown with one blast﴾ ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing﴾ ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ ﴿and the sky will split, for on that Day it will be frail﴾ ﴿and the angels will be upon its edges; and above them, on that Day, eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ ﴿on that Day you will be exposed; not a secret of yours will be concealed﴾. The fa' (then) here serves to link what follows to the terror with which the surah opened, from His saying ﴿The Inevitable Reality﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1] ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 2] ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3]. So it is understood that this is a terrifying description of the punishment with which the polytheists were threatened, of the kind that befell their likes in this world, and of the punishment of the Hereafter that awaits them. When He had completed the threat of punishment in this world, He followed it with a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, which befalls at the Striking Calamity that they denied, just as Thamud and 'Ad denied it. Thus there is an explanation of the Striking Calamity: that it is the Hour of Resurrection, which is the Event that occurs.

As for al-sur (the Trumpet): it is a horn of a bull that is hollowed out, and inside it a plug is placed that fills part of its emptiness, so that when a blower blows into it, the air is compressed and it produces a strong sound. Armies used to employ it to call one another when they wished to mobilize or to attack. This was discussed earlier, at His saying, ﴿And His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-An'am: 73], in Surat al-An'am.

The blowing into the Trumpet (al-nafkh fi al-sur) is an expression for the command of bringing into being, by reviving bodies for the Resurrection, like the reviving by the call of a group of soldiers charged with the horns to summon the rest of the army, where no soldier delays from coming to the place of the call. It may also be that there is an existent angel assigned to it who produces a powerful sound.

As for nafkhah (a blast): it is a verbal noun of nafakha, joined with a ta' indicating the single occurrence, i.e. unity. It is in origin an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), or it may stand in the place of the agent, since it is known that the one who blows is the angel assigned to blow the Trumpet, who is Israfil.

The description of nafkhah as wahidah (one) is an emphasis, to convey unity from the form of fa'lah, explicitly confirming the unity conveyed by the ta'.

The specification of this is to draw attention to the marvel at the influence upon all human bodies

[p. 125]
by a single blast, without repetition, marvelling at the great power of God and the efficacy of His command. For the context of the speech from the beginning of the surah is the terrifying of the Day of Resurrection, so enumerating its terrors is the aim. For the sake of directing attention to this here, the description wahidah is not mentioned in His saying, ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command; then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come forth﴾ [al-Rum: 25], in Surat al-Rum.

Thus from the mention of ﴿one blast﴾ results the emphasis of the meaning of blowing and the emphasis of the meaning of unity. This clarifies what was transmitted from the author of al-Kashshaf in his explanation with a general wording, transmitted by al-Tibi. The intent of describing it as wahidah is not that it is not followed by a second, for it has come in other verses that there are two blasts. Rather, the intent is that it does not need its repetition for the purpose to be achieved, as a metaphor for the swiftness of the occurrence of the Event, i.e. the Day of the Event.

As for the mention of the word nafkhah, it is so that the description of unity can be applied to it. The mention of nafkhah is a follower, not the subject of the speech. So this blast is the first, which heralds the end of the world; then the second blast occurs, which will be at the resurrection of the dead.

The clause ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted﴾ etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because the crushing of the earth and the mountains may occur before the blowing into the Trumpet, since by it the world passes away.

The meaning of hummilat (lifted): they are removed from their places, by the earth with its mountains being moved away from its usual orbit, so that they collide with other bodies in space and are crushed. This condition is likened to a carrier carrying something in order to throw it onto the ground, like the carrying of a ball between players. It is also possible that the action of the angels charged with disrupting the order of the world, upon the terrestrial sphere, by moving it away from its orbit, is likened to carrying. All of this occurs when the gravitational force, which God made to preserve the order of the world, becomes disturbed, up to a term known to God, exalted is He.

Al-dakk: a severe striking that breaks the struck object, i.e. when the parts of the earth and the parts of its mountains are scattered.

The verbs nufikha, hummilat and dukkata are in the passive voice, because the purpose is connected to explaining the object rather than the agent. The agent of those actions is either the angels or what God has placed in them of causes of those actions, all by God's permission and power.

[p. 126]
The clause ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ contains the answer to idha ("when"), namely His saying ﴿the Inevitable Event will occur﴾. As for His saying "then on that Day," it is an emphasis of the meaning of ﴿when the Trumpet is blown﴾ etc., because the tanwin of yawma'idhin is a replacement for a clause indicated by the clause ﴿is blown in the Trumpet﴾ up to His saying ﴿one crushing﴾; that is, "the day when the Trumpet is blown, to its end, the Inevitable Event will occur." It is a verbal emphasis with a synonym of the emphasized term, for the meaning of yawm in His saying ﴿then on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ is absolute time, as is generally the case when it is in construct with idha.

The meaning of ﴿the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ is the realization of what was expected to occur, for they were being threatened with a great event; on that Day what they were threatened with will be realized.

So He expressed it with the past tense, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence.

The meaning: then at that time the Event will occur.

Al-waqi'ah is synonymous with al-haqqah and al-qari'ah, so mentioning it explicitly in place of a pronoun serves to increase the terror and to convey the conditions indicated by the derivational sources of the descriptions al-haqqah, al-qari'ah and al-waqi'ah.

Al-waqi'ah has become a proper name by predominance in the terminology of the Qur'an for the Day of Resurrection. God said, ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1] ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 2].

The verb ﴿the sky will split﴾ [al-Rahman: 37] may be coordinated with the clause ﴿is blown in the Trumpet﴾, so that it is attached to the condition of idha, and the postponement of its coordination is because of what is joined to this splitting: the description of the angels surrounding it, and the mention of the Throne that encompasses the heavens and mention of its bearers.

It may also be a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause, with the estimate: "and the sky has split."

The splitting of the sky is its being affected by the verb of splitting. Shaqq is the opening of passages in its surface. God said, ﴿And on the Day the sky is split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25] ﴿The dominion that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan: 26].

Then it is possible that this is other than the splitting in His saying ﴿So when the sky is split and becomes red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], and it is possible that it is that same one.

[p. 127]
The literal meaning of wahiyah is weak and scattered, and wahy is used metaphorically for ease and lack of resistance; one says, "his resolve weakened" when he becomes lenient and yielding. In the proverb: "Weaker than the spider's web," said of a case where proof does not stand.

Its restriction to yawma'idhin indicates that the weakening came upon it after it had been firm through the cohesion of its parts, which is what the Qur'an expresses as ratq (joined), just as it expresses splitting as fatq (unjoining). That is, on that day it is opened and passable.

Wahy is close to wahn (weakness). Most often wahy is applied to non-rational things, and wahn is applied to people.

The meaning: the angels move back and forth through it, ascending and descending, contrary to its former condition. God said, ﴿So when the sky is split and becomes red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

The clause ﴿and the angel is upon its edges﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in fahiya; that is, on that day the angel is upon its edges.

Al-malak: its root meaning is one of the angels, and its definiteness here is the definiteness of the genus, and it carries the sense of plurality, i.e. the genus of angel, meaning a group of angels or all the angels if comprehensiveness is intended. The comprehensive sense of a singular noun is more explicit in indicating totality. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said, "al-Kitab is more than the books," and from it is His saying, ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened﴾ [Maryam: 4].

The pronoun in arja'iha refers to the sky.

The meaning: the angels work in the regions of the sky, carrying out the descent of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the driving of the people of Hellfire into the Fire.

ʿArsh al-Rabb: a name for what encompasses the heavens, and it is greater than the heavens.

By the eight who carry the Throne are meant eight of the angels. It was said: eight persons; it was said: eight rows; it was said: eight tenths, i.e. about eighty out of the total number of angels; and other things were said. This is among the unseen matters whose details are not the purpose,

[p. 128]
since the aim of the verse is to depict the greatness of God, exalted is He, and to bring that closer to understanding, as He said in other verses.

Perhaps the purpose of the allusion to what exceeds the admonition is that God taught His Prophet ﷺ some of those conditions by a symbolic method, through which understanding of their details is opened to him, and He did not intend to occupy us with knowledge of them.

It seems that the motive for mentioning them in summary is the transition to reporting about the Throne of God, so that its mention would not be abrupt after the mention of the angels.

al-Tirmidhi transmitted from al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, from the Prophet ﷺ, a hadith in which he mentioned the distances between the heavens. In the mention of the phrase "the Throne" there are symbols that al-Tirmidhi cited in the manner of an explanation of this verse. One of its narrators is 'Abdullah ibn 'Umayrah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays. al-Bukhari said: "We do not know that he heard from al-Ahnaf."

There are other reports besides the hadith of al-'Abbas that are not regarded. Ibn al-'Arabi said concerning them: they are fabrications from the People of the Book, or from the poetry of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, and it is not established that the Prophet ﷺ had it recited before him and affirmed it. End.

The pronoun in fawqahum refers to the angel.

fawqahum is connected to ﴿bears the Throne of your Lord﴾ and it is an emphasis of what the verb "bears" indicates of the Throne being elevated; it is thus in the position of the two restrictions in His saying, ﴿There is no creature on the earth nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ. The attribution of "Throne" to God is an attribution of honour, like the attribution of the Ka'bah to Him in His saying, ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], and God is exalted above sitting on the Throne and above dwelling in a house.

The address in His saying ("you will be exposed") is to all people, by the indication of the context and what follows of detail.

Al-'ard (exposition): its root meaning is passing things before one who wishes to examine them, like presenting merchandise to a buyer or reviewing an army before its commander. It is used here metaphorically for its necessary consequence, which is reckoning, while the literal meaning remains permissible.

[p. 129]
The meaning of ﴿not a secret of yours will be concealed﴾: nothing will be hidden from God or from His angels. The feminine form of khafiyah is because it is an adjective for a feminine noun understood either as an act of the servants, estimated as "a deed," or as "a soul," i.e. no soul's secret will be hidden from the reckoning, and no sinner will be confused with a believer, nor a righteous person with a wicked one.

The clause ﴿on that Day you will be exposed﴾ is a new sentence, or it is an explanation of the clause ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾, or it is a substitution of inclusion from it.

"Minkum" (of you) is a description of khafiyah, placed before it, so it is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

The repetition of "that Day" four times is to magnify that day, whose beginning is the blowing into the Trumpet, after which follows what is mentioned in the sentences after it. When He had completed the threat of punishment in this world, He followed it with a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, which befalls at the Striking Calamity that they denied, just as Thamud and 'Ad denied it.
