As for al-sur (the Trumpet): it is a horn of a bull that is hollowed out, and inside it a plug is placed that fills part of its emptiness, so that when a blower blows into it, the air is compressed and it produces a strong sound. Armies used to employ it to call one another when they wished to mobilize or to attack. This was discussed earlier, at His saying, ﴿And His is the dominion on the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-An'am: 73], in Surat al-An'am.

The blowing into the Trumpet (al-nafkh fi al-sur) is an expression for the command of bringing into being, by reviving bodies for the Resurrection, like the reviving by the call of a group of soldiers charged with the horns to summon the rest of the army, where no soldier delays from coming to the place of the call. It may also be that there is an existent angel assigned to it who produces a powerful sound.

As for nafkhah (a blast): it is a verbal noun of nafakha, joined with a ta' indicating the single occurrence, i.e. unity. It is in origin an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), or it may stand in the place of the agent, since it is known that the one who blows is the angel assigned to blow the Trumpet, who is Israfil.

The description of nafkhah as wahidah (one) is an emphasis, to convey unity from the form of fa'lah, explicitly confirming the unity conveyed by the ta'.

The specification of this is to draw attention to the marvel at the influence upon all human bodies

[p. 125]
by a single blast, without repetition, marvelling at the great power of God and the efficacy of His command. For the context of the speech from the beginning of the surah is the terrifying of the Day of Resurrection, so enumerating its terrors is the aim. For the sake of directing attention to this here, the description wahidah is not mentioned in His saying, ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command; then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come forth﴾ [al-Rum: 25], in Surat al-Rum.

Thus from the mention of ﴿one blast﴾ results the emphasis of the meaning of blowing and the emphasis of the meaning of unity. This clarifies what was transmitted from the author of al-Kashshaf in his explanation with a general wording, transmitted by al-Tibi. The intent of describing it as wahidah is not that it is not followed by a second, for it has come in other verses that there are two blasts. Rather, the intent is that it does not need its repetition for the purpose to be achieved, as a metaphor for the swiftness of the occurrence of the Event, i.e. the Day of the Event.

As for the mention of the word nafkhah, it is so that the description of unity can be applied to it. The mention of nafkhah is a follower, not the subject of the speech. So this blast is the first, which heralds the end of the world; then the second blast occurs, which will be at the resurrection of the dead.

The clause ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted﴾ etc. is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because the crushing of the earth and the mountains may occur before the blowing into the Trumpet, since by it the world passes away.

The meaning of hummilat (lifted): they are removed from their places, by the earth with its mountains being moved away from its usual orbit, so that they collide with other bodies in space and are crushed. This condition is likened to a carrier carrying something in order to throw it onto the ground, like the carrying of a ball between players. It is also possible that the action of the angels charged with disrupting the order of the world, upon the terrestrial sphere, by moving it away from its orbit, is likened to carrying. All of this occurs when the gravitational force, which God made to preserve the order of the world, becomes disturbed, up to a term known to God, exalted is He.

Al-dakk: a severe striking that breaks the struck object, i.e. when the parts of the earth and the parts of its mountains are scattered.

The verbs nufikha, hummilat and dukkata are in the passive voice, because the purpose is connected to explaining the object rather than the agent. The agent of those actions is either the angels or what God has placed in them of causes of those actions, all by God's permission and power.

[p. 126]
The clause ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ contains the answer to idha ("when"), namely His saying ﴿the Inevitable Event will occur﴾. As for His saying "then on that Day," it is an emphasis of the meaning of ﴿when the Trumpet is blown﴾ etc., because the tanwin of yawma'idhin is a replacement for a clause indicated by the clause ﴿is blown in the Trumpet﴾ up to His saying ﴿one crushing﴾; that is, "the day when the Trumpet is blown, to its end, the Inevitable Event will occur." It is a verbal emphasis with a synonym of the emphasized term, for the meaning of yawm in His saying ﴿then on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ is absolute time, as is generally the case when it is in construct with idha.

The meaning of ﴿the Inevitable Event will occur﴾ is the realization of what was expected to occur, for they were being threatened with a great event; on that Day what they were threatened with will be realized.

So He expressed it with the past tense, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence.

The meaning: then at that time the Event will occur.

Al-waqi'ah is synonymous with al-haqqah and al-qari'ah, so mentioning it explicitly in place of a pronoun serves to increase the terror and to convey the conditions indicated by the derivational sources of the descriptions al-haqqah, al-qari'ah and al-waqi'ah.

Al-waqi'ah has become a proper name by predominance in the terminology of the Qur'an for the Day of Resurrection. God said, ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1] ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 2].

The verb ﴿the sky will split﴾ [al-Rahman: 37] may be coordinated with the clause ﴿is blown in the Trumpet﴾, so that it is attached to the condition of idha, and the postponement of its coordination is because of what is joined to this splitting: the description of the angels surrounding it, and the mention of the Throne that encompasses the heavens and mention of its bearers.

It may also be a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause, with the estimate: "and the sky has split."

The splitting of the sky is its being affected by the verb of splitting. Shaqq is the opening of passages in its surface. God said, ﴿And on the Day the sky is split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25] ﴿The dominion that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Furqan: 26].

Then it is possible that this is other than the splitting in His saying ﴿So when the sky is split and becomes red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], and it is possible that it is that same one.

[p. 127]
The literal meaning of wahiyah is weak and scattered, and wahy is used metaphorically for ease and lack of resistance; one says, "his resolve weakened" when he becomes lenient and yielding. In the proverb: "Weaker than the spider's web," said of a case where proof does not stand.

Its restriction to yawma'idhin indicates that the weakening came upon it after it had been firm through the cohesion of its parts, which is what the Qur'an expresses as ratq (joined), just as it expresses splitting as fatq (unjoining). That is, on that day it is opened and passable.

Wahy is close to wahn (weakness). Most often wahy is applied to non-rational things, and wahn is applied to people.

The meaning: the angels move back and forth through it, ascending and descending, contrary to its former condition. God said, ﴿So when the sky is split and becomes red like tanned leather﴾ [al-Rahman: 37].

The clause ﴿and the angel is upon its edges﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in fahiya; that is, on that day the angel is upon its edges.

Al-malak: its root meaning is one of the angels, and its definiteness here is the definiteness of the genus, and it carries the sense of plurality, i.e. the genus of angel, meaning a group of angels or all the angels if comprehensiveness is intended. The comprehensive sense of a singular noun is more explicit in indicating totality. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said, "al-Kitab is more than the books," and from it is His saying, ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened﴾ [Maryam: 4].

The pronoun in arja'iha refers to the sky.

The meaning: the angels work in the regions of the sky, carrying out the descent of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the driving of the people of Hellfire into the Fire.

ʿArsh al-Rabb: a name for what encompasses the heavens, and it is greater than the heavens.

By the eight who carry the Throne are meant eight of the angels. It was said: eight persons; it was said: eight rows; it was said: eight tenths, i.e. about eighty out of the total number of angels; and other things were said. This is among the unseen matters whose details are not the purpose,

[p. 128]
since the aim of the verse is to depict the greatness of God, exalted is He, and to bring that closer to understanding, as He said in other verses.

Perhaps the purpose of the allusion to what exceeds the admonition is that God taught His Prophet ﷺ some of those conditions by a symbolic method, through which understanding of their details is opened to him, and He did not intend to occupy us with knowledge of them.

It seems that the motive for mentioning them in summary is the transition to reporting about the Throne of God, so that its mention would not be abrupt after the mention of the angels.

al-Tirmidhi transmitted from al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, from the Prophet ﷺ, a hadith in which he mentioned the distances between the heavens. In the mention of the phrase "the Throne" there are symbols that al-Tirmidhi cited in the manner of an explanation of this verse. One of its narrators is 'Abdullah ibn 'Umayrah, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays. al-Bukhari said: "We do not know that he heard from al-Ahnaf."

There are other reports besides the hadith of al-'Abbas that are not regarded. Ibn al-'Arabi said concerning them: they are fabrications from the People of the Book, or from the poetry of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, and it is not established that the Prophet ﷺ had it recited before him and affirmed it. End.

The pronoun in fawqahum refers to the angel.

fawqahum is connected to ﴿bears the Throne of your Lord﴾ and it is an emphasis of what the verb "bears" indicates of the Throne being elevated; it is thus in the position of the two restrictions in His saying, ﴿There is no creature on the earth nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ. The attribution of "Throne" to God is an attribution of honour, like the attribution of the Ka'bah to Him in His saying, ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], and God is exalted above sitting on the Throne and above dwelling in a house.

The address in His saying ("you will be exposed") is to all people, by the indication of the context and what follows of detail.

Al-'ard (exposition): its root meaning is passing things before one who wishes to examine them, like presenting merchandise to a buyer or reviewing an army before its commander. It is used here metaphorically for its necessary consequence, which is reckoning, while the literal meaning remains permissible.

[p. 129]
The meaning of ﴿not a secret of yours will be concealed﴾: nothing will be hidden from God or from His angels. The feminine form of khafiyah is because it is an adjective for a feminine noun understood either as an act of the servants, estimated as "a deed," or as "a soul," i.e. no soul's secret will be hidden from the reckoning, and no sinner will be confused with a believer, nor a righteous person with a wicked one.

The clause ﴿on that Day you will be exposed﴾ is a new sentence, or it is an explanation of the clause ﴿then, on that Day, the Inevitable Event will occur﴾, or it is a substitution of inclusion from it.

"Minkum" (of you) is a description of khafiyah, placed before it, so it is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

The repetition of "that Day" four times is to magnify that day, whose beginning is the blowing into the Trumpet, after which follows what is mentioned in the sentences after it. The mention of that day has occurred five times, because ﴿then on that Day the Event will occur﴾ repeats idha in His saying ﴿when the Trumpet is blown﴾; for the estimated complement of the annexed term in yawma'idhin is the meaning of the clause ﴿when the Trumpet is blown﴾. Thus the time of the blowing was mentioned first, and its mention was repeated after that four times.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿la tukhfa﴾ with a feminine (ta') prefix. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a masculine (ya') prefix, because the feminine marking of khafiyah is not real, and there is a separation between the verb and its subject.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 19–24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning."﴾ ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ ﴿whose fruits are within reach.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you advanced in the days gone by."﴾

The fa' (fa) here is an elaboration (tafsil) of what is implied by "you will be presented" (tu'radun), since the presentation (al-'ard) is a presentation for reckoning and recompense; so the giving of the record is the stopping of each one before the page of his deeds. And "amma" (amma) is a particle of elaboration and conditionality, and it conveys the meaning of "whatever may be the case" (mahma yakun min shay'), and the meaning is: whatever the presentation may be, the one who is given his record in his right hand is in a pleasing life. The custom of the fa' that links to its response is that it is separated from "amma" by a part of the response clause or by something connected to the response that is of concern; for when they were bound to omit the verb of the condition because it is merged into the meaning of "amma," they disliked the joining of the response-fa' to the conditional particle, so they separated between them with a separator, to beautify the form of the speech. Thus His saying ﴿the one who is given his record in his right hand﴾ originally is the opening of the response clause, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾, as will come.

His saying ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ indicates an omitted statement for brevity, its estimate being: "So every person will be given the record of his deeds; as for him who is given his record..." etc., following the manner of His saying: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63].

The ba' (ba') in His saying "in his right hand" is for accompaniment (musahaba) or in the sense of "in" (fi).

The giving of the record in the right hand is a sign that it is a giving of honour and good tidings. The Arabs mention taking with the right hand as a metonymy for care for what is taken and pride in it. Al-Shammakh said:

"When a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah receives it in the right hand."

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 27] ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28], the verse. Then He said: ﴿And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 41] ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 42], the verse.

The clause ﴿he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ is the response of the conditional "amma," and it takes the place of the predicate of the subject. This saying is the saying of one possessed of joy and delight, which prompts him to make people aware of what is in his record of deeds of recompense, in a station of exultation and pride; so in it is a metonymy for his being in delight and bliss, for the metonymic meaning is the more important purpose of mentioning the presentation.

"Hā'um" (ha'um) is composed of "hā'" (ha) extended and shortened (mamdud and maqsur). The extended form is built on opening the hamza when it is stripped of the signs of address except when addressed to a woman, in which case it is with a kasra on the hamza without a ya'. When it is addressed to more than one person, its extension is obligatory so that the sign of address can be attached, like the sign that attaches to the pronoun of the addressee, and they gave its hamza a damma like the damma of the pronoun of address, since the sign of the dual and plural attaches to it; so one says "hā'umā" as one says "antumā," and "hā'um" as one says "antum," and "hā'unna" as one says "antunna." Among the philologists is one who claimed that "hā'um" originally is "hā ummū," composed of two words, "hā" and an imperative verb for the group from the verb "amma" when intended, then it was lightened through frequent use; but this is not sound, because they have not heard "hā'umayn" in addressing a group of women. There are other dialects and usages concerning the attachment of the kāf of address to it, which al-Radi traced in his commentary on al-Kafiyah and Ibn Manzur in Lisan al-'Arab.

"Hā'um" in all its forms is considered a noun of the verb in the imperative meaning "take," as in al-Kashshaf, and also in the meaning "come," as in al-Nihayah.

The address in His saying ﴿Here, read!﴾ is to the righteous among the people of the gathering.

"Kitabiyah" originally is "kitabiya," with the ya' of the speaker being vowelled, according to one of the views concerning the ya' of the speaker when it falls as a possessed noun to it; this vowelling is, I think, intended to show the attachment of the possessed noun to that ya' at pause, preserving the vowel of the ya' which is intended to be brought out.

"Iqra'u" (read) is an explanation of the intended meaning of the noun of the verb in "hā'um."

Both "hā'um" and "iqra'u" have as their object "kitabiyah" (competition of governance). The estimate is: "Here, my record, read my record!" The hā' in "kitabiyah" and its like is for pause at the time of stopping.

The rule for this hā' is that it is to be kept in pause and dropped in continuation. It has been kept in this verse in both states according to the majority of the readers, and it is written in the codices; so it is known that it serves to express the reported speech in the language of that speaker with what is equivalent to it in Arabic usage, since the usage is that the speaker comes with this hā' at pause on both clauses.

And because these words came as fawasil (verse-endings), and the fawasil like the saj' are considered in their state of pause, like the rhymes; so if it were said, "Read my record! Indeed I was certain that I would meet my reckoning," two fawasil would drop away, and that would be a neglect of two embellishments.

Ya'qub read them in continuation with the hā' dropped, and the readers prefer that the reciter pause on them to agree with the well-known orthography of the codex and so that the beauty of the saj' is not lost.

The verb "zann" (to think/be certain) in His saying ﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning﴾ is used in the sense of certainty, which is one of its two meanings. It is related from al-Dahhak: every "zann" in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty, and from an unbeliever is doubt.

The real meaning of "zann" is knowledge that has not been verified; either because what is known by it has not yet occurred and has not come into the world of the senses, or because the knowledge of its possessor is mixed with doubt. By this, the use of "zann" for what is known with certainty is a truly literal usage. On this went al-Azhari in al-Tahdhib and Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Atiyyah confined himself to this meaning.

The words of al-Kashshaf indicate that the origin of "zann" is knowledge that is not certain, but it may take the place of knowledge, because the predominant opinion is placed in the position of knowledge in customs and rulings; and he said: it is said, "I think a thought like certainty that the matter is such and such." So for him, when it is used for certainty, it is a metaphor. This is also the view of al-Jawhari, Ibn Sidah and al-Fayruzabadi. As for His saying ﴿We only think a thought, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32], there is no evidence in it, because the indefiniteness of "zannan" is meant to indicate paucity, and it is emphasized by ﴿and we are not certain﴾, so it admits both possibilities. It has already been discussed under His saying ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-A'raf: 66] in Surat al-A'raf, and His saying ﴿and they thought that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118] in Surat Bara'ah.

The meaning is: "I knew in the world that I would meet the reckoning," that is, I believed in the resurrection. This statement is used as a metonymy for his readiness for the reckoning by advancing faith and righteous deeds, which were the cause of his happiness.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning﴾ is in the position of causal explanation for the joy and delight indicated by His saying ﴿Here, read my record!﴾; and thus the particle "inna" is for mere emphasis and to express causation.

The position of ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ is that of a consequence drawn from what preceded of his being given his record in his right hand and what resulted from that of gladness and honour at the gathering; so the fa' is for making the mention of this clause a consequence of the mention of what came before. You may also make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾, for that saying included that its speaker is in bliss, as already mentioned; and repeating the fa' with the clause is from repeating the governing element with the substituted element for emphasis, like His saying ﴿It will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114].

"Ta'ishah" (life) is the state and condition of living.

The description of "'ishah" as "radiyah" (pleasing) is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the life is associated with the state of its owner, the one who lives, in the way a description is associated with what it describes.

The one pleased is the owner of the life, not the life itself; for "radiyah" is the active participle of "radiya," when contentment (al-ridha), which is joy and gladness, has come to it.

The life is not pleased in itself, but because of its goodness its owner is pleased; so he described it as "radiyah" by attributing the description to other than what it belongs to, and this is part of exaggeration, for it indicates the intensity of the contentment through it, to the point that it has spread into it; and for this consideration al-Sakkaki returned what is called the intellectual metaphor to the implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), as mentioned in the science of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan).

The "fi" (in) here is for figurative location, which is association.

The clause ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ is a substitute of inclusion for the clause ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾.

"Al-'Uluww" is elevation, and it is one of the excellences of gardens, for its owner overlooks many directions with a wide view; and because many of the beauties of his garden appear to him when he looks at it from its top or middle, which would not appear to his sight had his garden been in flat land; and this is from the increase of joy and delight, for the beauty of views is among the pleasures of the soul and among the blessings. And it occurs in the poetry of Zuhayr:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a stricken [camel], from the water-carrying camels, were watering a garden, distant (suhuqan)."

The philologists said: it is permissible that "suhuqan" is an adjective of "jannah" without an estimate, as they said: "naqah 'ulut" (a she-camel without tail-hair) and "imra'ah 'utul" (a woman without adornment). They did not turn to the meaning of "sahaq" in it, which is elevation, because the elevated is distant; and they said: the date-palm "sahuqat" like "karuma," when it grew tall. And in the Qur'an: ﴿like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265].

They also permitted that "al-'uluww" may be intended as elevation of rank, like the saying "so-and-so has a lofty degree," and by this the word "'aliyah" here has a meaning that the phrase ﴿like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265] does not have, because what is meant there is a garden of this world.

"Al-qutuf" is the plural of "qitf," with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', and it means the fruit; it was so named because it is plucked (yuqtaf); and its origin is a noun in the sense of a passive participle, like "dhibh."

The meaning of its being near (dunuww) is its nearness to the hands of those who reach for it, for that is more pleasant, since there is no hardship in it; He the Exalted said: ﴿and its fruits will be made readily accessible, made easy﴾ [al-Insan: 14].

The clause ﴿Eat and drink﴾ to its end is a quoted speech of an omitted saying, and it together with what is quoted is in the position of a description of "jannah"; the estimate being: it will be said to the group who are given their records in their right hands when they settle in the garden: "Eat and drink," etc.

It is also permissible that the clause be a second predicate concerning the pronoun in His saying ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾.

The pronouns of the group who were given their records in their right hands were mentioned in the singular earlier, then the pronoun came in the plural when reporting their address, because those earlier pronouns were accompanied by verbs that apply to each individual of the group as he completes his reckoning. As for the pronoun of "eat and drink," it is an address to the whole group after they have settled in the garden, just as guests enter a banquet and each one entering is greeted with words specific to him; then when they have settled, their host approaches them with expressions of honour.

"Hani'an" (with satisfaction) may be a fa'il in the sense of an active participle when satisfaction is established for it, so it is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object, since it is its description; and attributing satisfaction to the eating and drinking is an intellectual metaphor, since they are both associated with satisfaction for the eater and drinker.

It is also permissible that it be an active participle from a non-triliteral form in a pattern of the triliteral; the estimate being "muhanni'an," i.e., a cause of satisfaction, as 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

"From Rayhanah, the caller who hears" — i.e., the one who makes hear;

and as Allah the Exalted is described as "al-Hakim" in the sense of the one who makes the creatures judged. It is also permissible that it be a fa'il in the sense of a passive participle, i.e., "mahni'an bihi" (that by which one is made content).

In all these possibilities, the singular form of "hani'an" while it is a description of two things, on the basis that fa'il in the sense of active participle does not agree with what it describes, or on the basis that if it is a description of a verbal noun, it stands in place of its described noun, and description by a verbal noun is not dualized, pluralized or feminized.

"Bima asslaftum" (for what you advanced) is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "eat and drink."

The "ba'" here is causal.

The referent of the relative "ma" is the deed, i.e., the righteous deed.

"Al-Islaf" is making a thing a salaf, i.e., something that precedes.

The meaning is that it is advanced and sent ahead in time so that it may be benefited from when there is need of it; and from it is derived "salaf" for a loan, "islaf" for lending, and "sulfah" for a salam (advance-sale).

The days that have passed (al-ayyam al-khaliyah): those that are past and far away. It is derived from al-khulluww (khuluww), which means being empty or vacant, and also being distant.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 19–24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning."﴾ ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ ﴿whose fruits are within reach.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you advanced in the days gone by."﴾

The fa' (fa) here is an elaboration (tafsil) of what is implied by "you will be presented" (tu'radun), since the presentation (al-'ard) is a presentation for reckoning and recompense; so the giving of the record is the stopping of each one before the page of his deeds. And "amma" (amma) is a particle of elaboration and conditionality, and it conveys the meaning of "whatever may be the case" (mahma yakun min shay'), and the meaning is: whatever the presentation may be, the one who is given his record in his right hand is in a pleasing life. The custom of the fa' that links to its response is that it is separated from "amma" by a part of the response clause or by something connected to the response that is of concern; for when they were bound to omit the verb of the condition because it is merged into the meaning of "amma," they disliked the joining of the response-fa' to the conditional particle, so they separated between them with a separator, to beautify the form of the speech. The "ba'" here is causal.

The referent of the relative "ma" is the deed, i.e., the righteous deed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 19–24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning."﴾ ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ ﴿whose fruits are within reach.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you advanced in the days gone by."﴾

The fa' (fa) here is an elaboration (tafsil) of what is implied by "you will be presented" (tu'radun), since the presentation (al-'ard) is a presentation for reckoning and recompense; so the giving of the record is the stopping of each one before the page of his deeds. And "amma" (amma) is a particle of elaboration and conditionality, and it conveys the meaning of "whatever may be the case" (mahma yakun min shay'), and the meaning is: whatever the presentation may be, the one who is given his record in his right hand is in a pleasing life. The custom of the fa' that links to its response is that it is separated from "amma" by a part of the response clause or by something connected to the response that is of concern; for when they were bound to omit the verb of the condition because it is merged into the meaning of "amma," they disliked the joining of the response-fa' to the conditional particle, so they separated between them with a separator, to beautify the form of the speech. Thus His saying ﴿the one who is given his record in his right hand﴾ originally is the opening of the response clause, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾, as will come.

His saying ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ indicates an omitted statement for brevity, its estimate being: "So every person will be given the record of his deeds; as for him who is given his record..." etc., following the manner of His saying: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63].

The ba' (ba') in His saying "in his right hand" is for accompaniment (musahaba) or in the sense of "in" (fi).

The giving of the record in the right hand is a sign that it is a giving of honour and good tidings. The Arabs mention taking with the right hand as a metonymy for care for what is taken and pride in it. Al-Shammakh said:

"When a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah receives it in the right hand."

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 27] ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28], the verse. Then He said: ﴿And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 41] ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 42], the verse.

The clause ﴿he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ is the response of the conditional "amma," and it takes the place of the predicate of the subject. This saying is the saying of one possessed of joy and delight, which prompts him to make people aware of what is in his record of deeds of recompense, in a station of exultation and pride; so in it is a metonymy for his being in delight and bliss, for the metonymic meaning is the more important purpose of mentioning the presentation.

"Hā'um" (ha'um) is composed of "hā'" (ha) extended and shortened (mamdud and maqsur). The extended form is built on opening the hamza when it is stripped of the signs of address except when addressed to a woman, in which case it is with a kasra on the hamza without a ya'. When it is addressed to more than one person, its extension is obligatory so that the sign of address can be attached, like the sign that attaches to the pronoun of the addressee, and they gave its hamza a damma like the damma of the pronoun of address, since the sign of the dual and plural attaches to it; so one says "hā'umā" as one says "antumā," and "hā'um" as one says "antum," and "hā'unna" as one says "antunna." Among the philologists is one who claimed that "hā'um" originally is "hā ummū," composed of two words, "hā" and an imperative verb for the group from the verb "amma" when intended, then it was lightened through frequent use; but this is not sound, because they have not heard "hā'umayn" in addressing a group of women. There are other dialects and usages concerning the attachment of the kāf of address to it, which al-Radi traced in his commentary on al-Kafiyah and Ibn Manzur in Lisan al-'Arab.

"Hā'um" in all its forms is considered a noun of the verb in the imperative meaning "take," as in al-Kashshaf, and also in the meaning "come," as in al-Nihayah.

The address in His saying ﴿Here, read!﴾ is to the righteous among the people of the gathering.

"Kitabiyah" originally is "kitabiya," with the ya' of the speaker being vowelled, according to one of the views concerning the ya' of the speaker when it falls as a possessed noun to it; this vowelling is, I think, intended to show the attachment of the possessed noun to that ya' at pause, preserving the vowel of the ya' which is intended to be brought out.

"Iqra'u" (read) is an explanation of the intended meaning of the noun of the verb in "hā'um."

Both "hā'um" and "iqra'u" have as their object "kitabiyah" (competition of governance). The estimate is: "Here, my record, read my record!" The hā' in "kitabiyah" and its like is for pause at the time of stopping.

The rule for this hā' is that it is to be kept in pause and dropped in continuation. It has been kept in this verse in both states according to the majority of the readers, and it is written in the codices; so it is known that it serves to express the reported speech in the language of that speaker with what is equivalent to it in Arabic usage, since the usage is that the speaker comes with this hā' at pause on both clauses.

And because these words came as fawasil (verse-endings), and the fawasil like the saj' are considered in their state of pause, like the rhymes; so if it were said, "Read my record! Indeed I was certain that I would meet my reckoning," two fawasil would drop away, and that would be a neglect of two embellishments.

Ya'qub read them in continuation with the hā' dropped, and the readers prefer that the reciter pause on them to agree with the well-known orthography of the codex and so that the beauty of the saj' is not lost.

The verb "zann" (to think/be certain) in His saying ﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning﴾ is used in the sense of certainty, which is one of its two meanings. It is related from al-Dahhak: every "zann" in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty, and from an unbeliever is doubt.

The real meaning of "zann" is knowledge that has not been verified; either because what is known by it has not yet occurred and has not come into the world of the senses, or because the knowledge of its possessor is mixed with doubt. By this, the use of "zann" for what is known with certainty is a truly literal usage. On this went al-Azhari in al-Tahdhib and Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Atiyyah confined himself to this meaning.

The words of al-Kashshaf indicate that the origin of "zann" is knowledge that is not certain, but it may take the place of knowledge, because the predominant opinion is placed in the position of knowledge in customs and rulings; and he said: it is said, "I think a thought like certainty that the matter is such and such." So for him, when it is used for certainty, it is a metaphor. This is also the view of al-Jawhari, Ibn Sidah and al-Fayruzabadi. As for His saying ﴿We only think a thought, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32], there is no evidence in it, because the indefiniteness of "zannan" is meant to indicate paucity, and it is emphasized by ﴿and we are not certain﴾, so it admits both possibilities. It has already been discussed under His saying ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-A'raf: 66] in Surat al-A'raf, and His saying ﴿and they thought that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118] in Surat Bara'ah.

The meaning is: "I knew in the world that I would meet the reckoning," that is, I believed in the resurrection. This statement is used as a metonymy for his readiness for the reckoning by advancing faith and righteous deeds, which were the cause of his happiness.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning﴾ is in the position of causal explanation for the joy and delight indicated by His saying ﴿Here, read my record!﴾; and thus the particle "inna" is for mere emphasis and to express causation.

The position of ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ is that of a consequence drawn from what preceded of his being given his record in his right hand and what resulted from that of gladness and honour at the gathering; so the fa' is for making the mention of this clause a consequence of the mention of what came before. You may also make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾, for that saying included that its speaker is in bliss, as already mentioned; and repeating the fa' with the clause is from repeating the governing element with the substituted element for emphasis, like His saying ﴿It will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114].

"Ta'ishah" (life) is the state and condition of living.

The description of "'ishah" as "radiyah" (pleasing) is an intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the life is associated with the state of its owner, the one who lives, in the way a description is associated with what it describes.

The one pleased is the owner of the life, not the life itself; for "radiyah" is the active participle of "radiya," when contentment (al-ridha), which is joy and gladness, has come to it.

The life is not pleased in itself, but because of its goodness its owner is pleased; so he described it as "radiyah" by attributing the description to other than what it belongs to, and this is part of exaggeration, for it indicates the intensity of the contentment through it, to the point that it has spread into it; and for this consideration al-Sakkaki returned what is called the intellectual metaphor to the implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), as mentioned in the science of rhetoric (ilm al-bayan).

The "fi" (in) here is for figurative location, which is association.

The clause ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ is a substitute of inclusion for the clause ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾.

"Al-'Uluww" is elevation, and it is one of the excellences of gardens, for its owner overlooks many directions with a wide view; and because many of the beauties of his garden appear to him when he looks at it from its top or middle, which would not appear to his sight had his garden been in flat land; and this is from the increase of joy and delight, for the beauty of views is among the pleasures of the soul and among the blessings. And it occurs in the poetry of Zuhayr:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a stricken [camel], from the water-carrying camels, were watering a garden, distant (suhuqan)."

The philologists said: it is permissible that "suhuqan" is an adjective of "jannah" without an estimate, as they said: "naqah 'ulut" (a she-camel without tail-hair) and "imra'ah 'utul" (a woman without adornment). They did not turn to the meaning of "sahaq" in it, which is elevation, because the elevated is distant; and they said: the date-palm "sahuqat" like "karuma," when it grew tall. And in the Qur'an: ﴿like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265].

They also permitted that "al-'uluww" may be intended as elevation of rank, like the saying "so-and-so has a lofty degree," and by this the word "'aliyah" here has a meaning that the phrase ﴿like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265] does not have, because what is meant there is a garden of this world.

"Al-qutuf" is the plural of "qitf," with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', and it means the fruit; it was so named because it is plucked (yuqtaf); and its origin is a noun in the sense of a passive participle, like "dhibh."

The meaning of its being near (dunuww) is its nearness to the hands of those who reach for it, for that is more pleasant, since there is no hardship in it; He the Exalted said: ﴿and its fruits will be made readily accessible, made easy﴾ [al-Insan: 14].

The clause ﴿Eat and drink﴾ to its end is a quoted speech of an omitted saying, and it together with what is quoted is in the position of a description of "jannah"; the estimate being: it will be said to the group who are given their records in their right hands when they settle in the garden: "Eat and drink," etc.

It is also permissible that the clause be a second predicate concerning the pronoun in His saying ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾.

The pronouns of the group who were given their records in their right hands were mentioned in the singular earlier, then the pronoun came in the plural when reporting their address, because those earlier pronouns were accompanied by verbs that apply to each individual of the group as he completes his reckoning. As for the pronoun of "eat and drink," it is an address to the whole group after they have settled in the garden, just as guests enter a banquet and each one entering is greeted with words specific to him; then when they have settled, their host approaches them with expressions of honour.

"Hani'an" (with satisfaction) may be a fa'il in the sense of an active participle when satisfaction is established for it, so it is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object, since it is its description; and attributing satisfaction to the eating and drinking is an intellectual metaphor, since they are both associated with satisfaction for the eater and drinker.

"From Rayhanah, the caller who hears" — i.e., the one who makes hear;

and as Allah the Exalted is described as "al-Hakim" in the sense of the one who makes the creatures judged. It is also permissible that it be a fa'il in the sense of a passive participle, i.e., "mahni'an bihi" (that by which one is made content).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 25–29:

﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record, and had not known what my account is! Oh, I wish it had been the end [of me]! My wealth has not availed me. My authority has gone from me."﴾ This is the counterpart of ﴿him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19]. Therefore, the discussion of his being given his record in his left hand has already been clarified by what preceded.

The wish of everyone who is given his record in his left hand is that he had not been given his record, because from looking into his record he knew that he was heading toward punishment, so he wishes that he had not known this, in order to spare himself the grief of it for a time, since anticipating evil is itself a punishment.

The clause ﴿and had not known what my account is﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun in (laytanī).

The meaning is that he used to deny the reckoning, which is the counterpart of the statement of the one given his record in his right hand: "Indeed, I thought that I would meet my account" [al-Haqqah: 20].

The circumstantial clause is parenthetical between the two clauses of the wish.

It is also possible that it is coordinated with the wish, i.e., "Oh, I wish I had not known what my account is," meaning I did not know the reality of my account, i.e., its outcome. Although this is in the sense of the wish preceding it, its repetition serves to express regret and sorrow.

The (mā) is interrogative, and the interrogation with it is what suspends the verb (adri) from taking an object. The clause ﴿Oh, I wish it had been the end [of me]﴾ is another wish, and it is not coordinated with the first wish, because the intent is expression of grief and remorse.

The pronoun in (laytahā) refers to something understood from the context, i.e., "Oh, I wish my state had been the end," or "Oh, I wish my calamity had been the end."

Al-qāḍiyah (the end) means death, which is the meaning of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And the disbeliever will say: "Oh, I wish I had been dust!"﴾ [al-Naba': 40], i.e., buried in the dust.

The clause ﴿Oh, I wish it had been the end [of me]﴾ is among the speech suitable to serve as a proverb, for its brevity, abundance of meaning, and elegance of sense. He expresses through it what the one given his record in his left hand says of regret, using the expression that the one regretting in this world would use, in Arabic speech that conveys the intended meaning. Its counterpart is what is related of them in His statement: ﴿There they will call for destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 13], and His statement ﴿"Oh, woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend"﴾ [al-Furqan: 28], and His statement ﴿"Oh, woe to us! What is this book?"﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], and the verse.

Then he began to lament what he had neglected of good in the world by turning to what he did not find in the eternal world, so he said: ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾, i.e., this is said by whoever among that group, from all the people of association and disbelief, had wealth and authority. So consider the regret of those who followed them and imitated them when they see them in such a state. In this there is an allusion to the chiefs of the idolaters of the Arabs, such as Abu Jahl and Umayyah ibn Khalaf. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, possessors of luxury﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

In ﴿aghnā 'annī﴾ there is khaṭṭī paronomasia (jinās khaṭṭī), even with slight difference, as in their saying: "Your pride deceived you, so its final outcome became your humiliation" (gharraka ʿizzuka fa-ṣāra quṣārā dhālika dhulluka).

The meaning of the ruin of authority is its being of no benefit on that day, so it is a metaphorical ruin. (Halaka) is construed with the sense of (ghāba) (was absent), and so it takes (ʿan), i.e., my authority that I had known did not appear to me.

The discussion of the (hāʾ) endings in "kitābiyah, ḥisābiyah, mālīyah, sulṭānīyah" is like the discussion of what preceded, except that Ḥamzah and Khalaf read here (mā aghnā ʿannī mālīyah, halaka ʿannī sulṭānīyah) without the hāʾ in pausal-connected recitation (ḥālat al-waṣl).

The circumstantial clause is parenthetical between the two clauses of the wish.

[Page 137]

(Seize him) is a verb of speech (maqūl) for an omitted saying, and its position is that of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿فَيَقُولُ يا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُوتَ كِتابِيَهْ﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 25]. The sense is: "It will be said: Seize him!"

From the context it is known that those commanded to seize him are the angels entrusted with driving the people of reckoning to what has been prepared for them.

al-akhdh (seizing) is holding with the hand.

Ghulluhu (shackle him) is the imperative of ghalla, meaning to place him in a ghull (shackle), the restraint placed on the neck of a criminal or a captive. It is a verb derived from a solid noun (ism jāmid) and is only attested in its triliteral form. Its regular form might have been ghallalahu with two lams, since ghull has a doubled lam, and it would be like ʿammama (to put a turban on someone), azzara (to clothe someone with a waist-wrap), and darraʿa al-jāriya (to dress a girl in a coat of mail). Perhaps they said ghallahu for lightness. The particle fa, which indicates immediate sequence, is used to express haste in putting him into the shackles right after seizing him.

(Then) in ﴿ثُمَّ الجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ﴾ indicates sequence in rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), because what the clause it introduces expresses is more severe punishment than seizing him and putting him in shackles.

Ṣallū (burn him) is a verb of the doubled form used for causative transitivity (taḍʿīf taʿdiya). ṣalā al-nār originally means it touched him with its heat or he warmed himself by it. When made transitive one says aṣlāhu nāran and ṣallāhu nāran.

(Then) in ﴿ثُمَّ في سِلْسِلَةٍ ذَرْعُها سَبْعُونَ ذِراعًا فاسْلُكُوهُ﴾ indicates sequence in rank with respect to the content of the two clauses before it, because what ﴿in a chain seventy cubits long﴾ expresses is greater than what (fa-ghulluhu) expresses.

The content of (fa-uslukūhu) indicates his being placed into Hellfire, so threading him into that chain is greater than merely threading him into Hellfire in general.

The meaning of (uslukūhu) is: make him a traverser (sālik), that is, one who enters the chain. This is done by winding the chain around him so that he is in its midst. One says salakahu when he causes him to enter something. That is, put him in the Fire bound in his shackles.

[Page 138]

The placing of (al-Jaḥīm) before its governing verb is for hastening the distress, while also observing the rhyme (al-fāṣila, the verse-ending). Likewise the placing of ﴿في سِلْسِلَةٍ﴾ before its governing verb.

The verb (uslukūhu) is connected with fa either as an emphasis of the fa that accompanied (fa-ghulluhu), or to signal that the verb is treated as the response of an omitted conditional clause. This omission is generally suggested by the fronting of the object, as if it were said: "Whatever you do to him, thread him into a chain," or "Whatever it may be, thread him."

The purpose is to affirm the occurrence of this, to urge against negligence in carrying it out, and to indicate that no lightening of it is to be hoped for. A parallel is the Almighty's saying ﴿ورَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3] ﴿وثِيابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 4] ﴿والرُّجْزَ فاهْجُرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 5]. This was discussed at His saying ﴿قُلْ بِفَضْلِ اللَّهِ وبِرَحْمَتِهِ فَبِذَلِكَ فَلْيَفْرَحُوا﴾ [Yūnus: 58] in Surat Yūnus.

al-Silsila (the chain) is a name for a collection of iron rings, some of which are interlocked with others, used to bind a person so that he does not move from his place. It was discussed at the Almighty's saying ﴿إذِ الأغْلالُ في أعْناقِهِمْ والسَّلاسِلُ﴾ [Ghāfir: 71] in Surat Ghāfir.

The clause ﴿ذَرْعُها سَبْعُونَ ذِراعًا﴾ is an attribute (ṣifa) of (silsila). This attribute occurs as an interjected element between the genitive (majrūr) and what it depends on, for the purpose of terrifying the polytheists who denied the Striking Calamity (al-Qāriʿa). The clause is not something addressed to the angels entrusted with driving the criminals to punishment. For this reason, the number seventy is used to mean abundance, by way of metonymy (kināya), like the Almighty's saying ﴿إنْ تَسْتَغْفِرْ لَهم سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً فَلَنْ يَغْفِرَ اللَّهُ لَهُمْ﴾ [al-Tawba: 80].

al-Dharʿ (cubit) is the measuring of the length of a body by the forearm (dhirāʿ). It is a measure of length determined by the forearm of a human being. The people used to measure by the measures of body parts, such as the forearm (dhirāʿ), the finger (iṣbuʿ), the phalanx (unmula), and the foot (qadam), and by the distances between body parts, such as the span (shibr), the fitr, the rutab (with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and the tāʾ), the ʿatab, the buṣm, and the stride (khuṭwa).

The clause ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ لا يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ العَظِيمِ﴾ and ﴿ولا يَحُضُّ عَلى طَعامِ المِسْكِينِ﴾ is in the position of the reason (ʿilla) for the command to seize him and to burn him in Hellfire.

The description of God as ʿAẓīm (the Mighty) here is an allusion to the appropriateness of the greatness of the punishment to the sin, since the sin was ingratitude toward the Mighty, so the recompense was a fitting one.

[Page 139]

To urge (ḥaḍḍ) on something means to ask someone to do something and to press insistently in that request.

Negating his urging of the feeding of the needy implies, by way of implication (fahwā, a fortiori), that he does not feed the needy from his wealth. For if he does not command others to feed the needy, then he certainly does not feed them from his own property. So the meaning is: he does not feed the needy and does not command their feeding. The people of the pre-Islamic age (ahl al-jāhiliyya) used to give food at feasts, in gambling, to guests, and in the bonds of friendship, out of showing off and seeking reputation, and they fed the poor only a little among themselves. The not urging of the feeding of the needy has been made into hyperbole (mubālagha) regarding this person's stinginess toward the needy with the wealth of others, and a metonymy (kināya) for his stinginess toward them with his own wealth. Likewise, eagerness to feed a guest has been made a metonymy for generosity in the words of Zaynab bint al-Ṭaṯariyya lamenting her brother Yazīd:

When guests alight, he becomes a sour-tempered man among the tribe, until his cooking pots are set aside for them.

She means that he comes to the tribe and hurries them, to half the pots for the guests, until the tribe's pots are placed on the three stones and they begin cooking. al-ʿAdhawwar (a sour-tempered man), with an unpointed ʿayn and a pointed dhāl, is like ʿamalless: one of difficult disposition.

However, the metonymy in the verse for stinginess is stronger than the metonymy in the line for generosity, because the entailment in the verse is established by way of priority (awlawiyya), unlike in the line.

Since the non-urging of the feeding of the needy has been made part of the cause for the severity of his punishment, we learn from this an admonition for the believers, deterring them from withholding from the needy their right in property, which is the known right in zakat, expiations (kaffārāt), and other things.

The Almighty's saying ﴿فَلَيْسَ لَهُ اليَوْمَ هاهُنا حَمِيمٌ﴾ is part of the speech that began with (seize him), and is a consequence (tafrīʿ) of it.

Its purpose is that whoever is given his book in his left hand should hear it and despair of finding anyone to defend him by intercession. It is also a rebuke to him for what he squandered in his life of seeking favor with the idols and their custodians, and of their deceiving him into thinking they would be there for him in times of hardship and calamity. This is the reason for restricting the negation of a loyal friend with (today), as an allusion that their relatives in the world will not benefit them today, as He said ﴿ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا أيْنَ شُرَكاؤُكُمُ الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 22], and His saying concerning them ﴿فَهَلْ لَنا مِن شُفَعاءَ فَيَشْفَعُوا لَنا﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 53], and other things that are numerous in the verses of the Qur'an.

[Page 140]

So His saying (lahu) is the predicate (khabar) of (laysa), because the genitive with the lām of exclusivity (lām al-ikhtiṣāṣ) is the focus of the predication, not the adverb of place. His saying (hāhunā) is an adverb of place related to the implied being (al-kawn al-manwī) in the predicate by way of the preposition. This is preferable to making (hāhunā) the predicate of (laysa) and making (lahu) an attribute of (ḥamīm), since there is no need for this attribution.

al-Ḥamīm is the close relative. Here it is a metonymy for the helper, since it is well known among the Arabs that a person's helpers are his clan and tribe.

﴿ولا طَعامٌ﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with (ḥamīm).

al-Ghislīn, with a kasra on the ghayn, is what enters the mouths of the people of the Fire of the flowing matters from the bodies, the water of the Fire, and the like, of what God knows. It is a proper name for this, like sijjīn, sirqīn, and ʿirnīn. It has been said that it is on the pattern fiʿlīn from the root ghasl (washing), because it flows from the bodies as if it were washed away from them. There is no need to explain its derivation.

al-Khāṭiʾūn are the possessors of sins. One says khaṭiʾa when he commits a sin.

The meaning is: none eat it except he and his like among the sinners.

The definite form (al-khāṭiʾūn) is for indicating perfection in the description, that is, those who commit the gravest error, which is associating partners with God.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read (al-khāṭiʾūn) with the hamza pronounced. The clause ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ لا يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ العَظِيمِ﴾ and ﴿ولا يَحُضُّ عَلى طَعامِ المِسْكِينِ﴾ is in the position of the reason (ʿilla) for the command to seize him and to burn him in Hellfire.

The description of God as ʿAẓīm (the Mighty) here is an allusion to the appropriateness of the greatness of the punishment to the sin, since the sin was ingratitude toward the Mighty, so the recompense was a fitting one.

[Page 139]

To urge (ḥaḍḍ) on something means to ask someone to do something and to press insistently in that request.

Negating his urging of the feeding of the needy implies, by way of implication (fahwā, a fortiori), that he does not feed the needy from his wealth. For if he does not command others to feed the needy, then he certainly does not feed them from his own property. So the meaning is: he does not feed the needy and does not command their feeding. The people of the pre-Islamic age (ahl al-jāhiliyya) used to give food at feasts, in gambling, to guests, and in the bonds of friendship, out of showing off and seeking reputation, and they fed the poor only a little among themselves. The not urging of the feeding of the needy has been made into hyperbole (mubālagha) regarding this person's stinginess toward the needy with the wealth of others, and a metonymy (kināya) for his stinginess toward them with his own wealth. Likewise, eagerness to feed a guest has been made a metonymy for generosity in the words of Zaynab bint al-Ṭaṯariyya lamenting her brother Yazīd:

When guests alight, he becomes a sour-tempered man among the tribe, until his cooking pots are set aside for them.

She means that he comes to the tribe and hurries them, to half the pots for the guests, until the tribe's pots are placed on the three stones and they begin cooking. al-ʿAdhawwar (a sour-tempered man), with an unpointed ʿayn and a pointed dhāl, is like ʿamalless: one of difficult disposition.

However, the metonymy in the verse for stinginess is stronger than the metonymy in the line for generosity, because the entailment in the verse is established by way of priority (awlawiyya), unlike in the line.

Since the non-urging of the feeding of the needy has been made part of the cause for the severity of his punishment, we learn from this an admonition for the believers, deterring them from withholding from the needy their right in property, which is the known right in zakat, expiations (kaffārāt), and other things.

The Almighty's saying ﴿فَلَيْسَ لَهُ اليَوْمَ هاهُنا حَمِيمٌ﴾ is part of the speech that began with (seize him), and is a consequence (tafrīʿ) of it.

Its purpose is that whoever is given his book in his left hand should hear it and despair of finding anyone to defend him by intercession. It is also a rebuke to him for what he squandered in his life of seeking favor with the idols and their custodians, and of their deceiving him into thinking they would be there for him in times of hardship and calamity. This is the reason for restricting the negation of a loyal friend with (today), as an allusion that their relatives in the world will not benefit them today, as He said ﴿ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا أيْنَ شُرَكاؤُكُمُ الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 22], and His saying concerning them ﴿فَهَلْ لَنا مِن شُفَعاءَ فَيَشْفَعُوا لَنا﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 53], and other things that are numerous in the verses of the Qur'an.

[Page 140]

So His saying (lahu) is the predicate (khabar) of (laysa), because the genitive with the lām of exclusivity (lām al-ikhtiṣāṣ) is the focus of the predication, not the adverb of place. His saying (hāhunā) is an adverb of place related to the implied being (al-kawn al-manwī) in the predicate by way of the preposition. This is preferable to making (hāhunā) the predicate of (laysa) and making (lahu) an attribute of (ḥamīm), since there is no need for this attribution.

al-Ḥamīm is the close relative. Here it is a metonymy for the helper, since it is well known among the Arabs that a person's helpers are his clan and tribe.

﴿ولا طَعامٌ﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with (ḥamīm).

al-Ghislīn, with a kasra on the ghayn, is what enters the mouths of the people of the Fire of the flowing matters from the bodies, the water of the Fire, and the like, of what God knows. It is a proper name for this, like sijjīn, sirqīn, and ʿirnīn. It has been said that it is on the pattern fiʿlīn from the root ghasl (washing), because it flows from the bodies as if it were washed away from them. There is no need to explain its derivation.

al-Khāṭiʾūn are the possessors of sins. One says khaṭiʾa when he commits a sin.

The meaning is: none eat it except he and his like among the sinners.

The definite form (al-khāṭiʾūn) is for indicating perfection in the description, that is, those who commit the gravest error, which is associating partners with God.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read (al-khāṭiʾūn) with the hamza pronounced. Abū Jaʿfar read (al-khāṭūn) with a ḍamma on the ṭāʾ followed by a wāw, dropping the hamza for lightness after changing it to a yāʾ for lightness. al-Ṭībī said: Ḥamza, when pausing, read (al-khāṭīūn) by changing the hamza to a yāʾ, and only al-Ṭībī mentions this from him.

[Page 137]

(Seize him) is a verb of speech (maqūl) for an omitted saying, and its position is that of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿فَيَقُولُ يا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُوتَ كِتابِيَهْ﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 25]. The sense is: "It will be said: Seize him!"

From the context it is known that those commanded to seize him are the angels entrusted with driving the people of reckoning to what has been prepared for them.

al-akhdh (seizing) is holding with the hand.

Ghulluhu (shackle him) is the imperative of ghalla, meaning to place him in a ghull (shackle), the restraint placed on the neck of a criminal or a captive. It is a verb derived from a solid noun (ism jāmid) and is only attested in its triliteral form. Its regular form might have been ghallalahu with two lams, since ghull has a doubled lam, and it would be like ʿammama (to put a turban on someone), azzara (to clothe someone with a waist-wrap), and darraʿa al-jāriya (to dress a girl in a coat of mail). Perhaps they said ghallahu for lightness. The particle fa, which indicates immediate sequence, is used to express haste in putting him into the shackles right after seizing him.

(Then) in ﴿ثُمَّ الجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ﴾ indicates sequence in rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), because what the clause it introduces expresses is more severe punishment than seizing him and putting him in shackles.

Ṣallū (burn him) is a verb of the doubled form used for causative transitivity (taḍʿīf taʿdiya). ṣalā al-nār originally means it touched him with its heat or he warmed himself by it. When made transitive one says aṣlāhu nāran and ṣallāhu nāran.

(Then) in ﴿ثُمَّ في سِلْسِلَةٍ ذَرْعُها سَبْعُونَ ذِراعًا فاسْلُكُوهُ﴾ indicates sequence in rank with respect to the content of the two clauses before it, because what ﴿in a chain seventy cubits long﴾ expresses is greater than what (fa-ghulluhu) expresses.

The content of (fa-uslukūhu) indicates his being placed into Hellfire, so threading him into that chain is greater than merely threading him into Hellfire in general.

The meaning of (uslukūhu) is: make him a traverser (sālik), that is, one who enters the chain. This is done by winding the chain around him so that he is in its midst. One says salakahu when he causes him to enter something. That is, put him in the Fire bound in his shackles.

[Page 138]

The placing of (al-Jaḥīm) before its governing verb is for hastening the distress, while also observing the rhyme (al-fāṣila, the verse-ending). Likewise the placing of ﴿في سِلْسِلَةٍ﴾ before its governing verb.

The verb (uslukūhu) is connected with fa either as an emphasis of the fa that accompanied (fa-ghulluhu), or to signal that the verb is treated as the response of an omitted conditional clause. This omission is generally suggested by the fronting of the object, as if it were said: "Whatever you do to him, thread him into a chain," or "Whatever it may be, thread him."

The purpose is to affirm the occurrence of this, to urge against negligence in carrying it out, and to indicate that no lightening of it is to be hoped for. A parallel is the Almighty's saying ﴿ورَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3] ﴿وثِيابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 4] ﴿والرُّجْزَ فاهْجُرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 5]. This was discussed at His saying ﴿قُلْ بِفَضْلِ اللَّهِ وبِرَحْمَتِهِ فَبِذَلِكَ فَلْيَفْرَحُوا﴾ [Yūnus: 58] in Surat Yūnus.

al-Silsila (the chain) is a name for a collection of iron rings, some of which are interlocked with others, used to bind a person so that he does not move from his place. It was discussed at the Almighty's saying ﴿إذِ الأغْلالُ في أعْناقِهِمْ والسَّلاسِلُ﴾ [Ghāfir: 71] in Surat Ghāfir.

The clause ﴿ذَرْعُها سَبْعُونَ ذِراعًا﴾ is an attribute (ṣifa) of (silsila). This attribute occurs as an interjected element between the genitive (majrūr) and what it depends on, for the purpose of terrifying the polytheists who denied the Striking Calamity (al-Qāriʿa). The clause is not something addressed to the angels entrusted with driving the criminals to punishment. Its regular form might have been ghallalahu with two lams, since ghull has a doubled lam, and it would be like ʿammama (to put a turban on someone), azzara (to clothe someone with a waist-wrap), and darraʿa al-jāriya (to dress a girl in a coat of mail). Perhaps they said ghallahu for lightness. The particle fa, which indicates immediate sequence, is used to express haste in putting him into the shackles right after seizing him.

(Then) in ﴿ثُمَّ الجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ﴾ indicates sequence in rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), because what the clause it introduces expresses is more severe punishment than seizing him and putting him in shackles.

Ṣallū (burn him) is a verb of the doubled form used for causative transitivity (taḍʿīf taʿdiya). ṣalā al-nār originally means it touched him with its heat or he warmed himself by it. When made transitive one says aṣlāhu nāran and ṣallāhu nāran.

(Then) in ﴿ثُمَّ في سِلْسِلَةٍ ذَرْعُها سَبْعُونَ ذِراعًا فاسْلُكُوهُ﴾ indicates sequence in rank with respect to the content of the two clauses before it, because what ﴿in a chain seventy cubits long﴾ expresses is greater than what (fa-ghulluhu) expresses.

The content of (fa-uslukūhu) indicates his being placed into Hellfire, so threading him into that chain is greater than merely threading him into Hellfire in general.

The meaning of (uslukūhu) is: make him a traverser (sālik), that is, one who enters the chain. This is done by winding the chain around him so that he is in its midst. One says salakahu when he causes him to enter something. That is, put him in the Fire bound in his shackles.

[Page 138]

The placing of (al-Jaḥīm) before its governing verb is for hastening the distress, while also observing the rhyme (al-fāṣila, the verse-ending). Likewise the placing of ﴿في سِلْسِلَةٍ﴾ before its governing verb.

The verb (uslukūhu) is connected with fa either as an emphasis of the fa that accompanied (fa-ghulluhu), or to signal that the verb is treated as the response of an omitted conditional clause. This omission is generally suggested by the fronting of the object, as if it were said: "Whatever you do to him, thread him into a chain," or "Whatever it may be, thread him."

The purpose is to affirm the occurrence of this, to urge against negligence in carrying it out, and to indicate that no lightening of it is to be hoped for. A parallel is the Almighty's saying ﴿ورَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3] ﴿وثِيابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 4] ﴿والرُّجْزَ فاهْجُرْ﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 5]. This was discussed at His saying ﴿قُلْ بِفَضْلِ اللَّهِ وبِرَحْمَتِهِ فَبِذَلِكَ فَلْيَفْرَحُوا﴾ [Yūnus: 58] in Surat Yūnus.

al-Silsila (the chain) is a name for a collection of iron rings, some of which are interlocked with others, used to bind a person so that he does not move from his place. It was discussed at the Almighty's saying ﴿إذِ الأغْلالُ في أعْناقِهِمْ والسَّلاسِلُ﴾ [Ghāfir: 71] in Surat Ghāfir.

The clause ﴿ذَرْعُها سَبْعُونَ ذِراعًا﴾ is an attribute (ṣifa) of (silsila). This attribute occurs as an interjected element between the genitive (majrūr) and what it depends on, for the purpose of terrifying the polytheists who denied the Striking Calamity (al-Qāriʿa). The clause is not something addressed to the angels entrusted with driving the criminals to punishment. For this reason, the number seventy is used to mean abundance, by way of metonymy (kināya), like the Almighty's saying ﴿إنْ تَسْتَغْفِرْ لَهم سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً فَلَنْ يَغْفِرَ اللَّهُ لَهُمْ﴾ [al-Tawba: 80].

al-Dharʿ (cubit) is the measuring of the length of a body by the forearm (dhirāʿ). It is a measure of length determined by the forearm of a human being. The people used to measure by the measures of body parts, such as the forearm (dhirāʿ), the finger (iṣbuʿ), the phalanx (unmula), and the foot (qadam), and by the distances between body parts, such as the span (shibr), the fitr, the rutab (with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and the tāʾ), the ʿatab, the buṣm, and the stride (khuṭwa).

The clause ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ لا يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ العَظِيمِ﴾ and ﴿ولا يَحُضُّ عَلى طَعامِ المِسْكِينِ﴾ is in the position of the reason (ʿilla) for the command to seize him and to burn him in Hellfire.

The description of God as ʿAẓīm (the Mighty) here is an allusion to the appropriateness of the greatness of the punishment to the sin, since the sin was ingratitude toward the Mighty, so the recompense was a fitting one.

[Page 139]

To urge (ḥaḍḍ) on something means to ask someone to do something and to press insistently in that request.

Negating his urging of the feeding of the needy implies, by way of implication (fahwā, a fortiori), that he does not feed the needy from his wealth. For if he does not command others to feed the needy, then he certainly does not feed them from his own property. So the meaning is: he does not feed the needy and does not command their feeding. The people of the pre-Islamic age (ahl al-jāhiliyya) used to give food at feasts, in gambling, to guests, and in the bonds of friendship, out of showing off and seeking reputation, and they fed the poor only a little among themselves. The not urging of the feeding of the needy has been made into hyperbole (mubālagha) regarding this person's stinginess toward the needy with the wealth of others, and a metonymy (kināya) for his stinginess toward them with his own wealth. Likewise, eagerness to feed a guest has been made a metonymy for generosity in the words of Zaynab bint al-Ṭaṯariyya lamenting her brother Yazīd:

When guests alight, he becomes a sour-tempered man among the tribe, until his cooking pots are set aside for them.

She means that he comes to the tribe and hurries them, to half the pots for the guests, until the tribe's pots are placed on the three stones and they begin cooking. al-ʿAdhawwar (a sour-tempered man), with an unpointed ʿayn and a pointed dhāl, is like ʿamalless: one of difficult disposition.

However, the metonymy in the verse for stinginess is stronger than the metonymy in the line for generosity, because the entailment in the verse is established by way of priority (awlawiyya), unlike in the line.

Since the non-urging of the feeding of the needy has been made part of the cause for the severity of his punishment, we learn from this an admonition for the believers, deterring them from withholding from the needy their right in property, which is the known right in zakat, expiations (kaffārāt), and other things.

The Almighty's saying ﴿فَلَيْسَ لَهُ اليَوْمَ هاهُنا حَمِيمٌ﴾ is part of the speech that began with (seize him), and is a consequence (tafrīʿ) of it.

Its purpose is that whoever is given his book in his left hand should hear it and despair of finding anyone to defend him by intercession. It is also a rebuke to him for what he squandered in his life of seeking favor with the idols and their custodians, and of their deceiving him into thinking they would be there for him in times of hardship and calamity. This is the reason for restricting the negation of a loyal friend with (today), as an allusion that their relatives in the world will not benefit them today, as He said ﴿ثُمَّ نَقُولُ لِلَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا أيْنَ شُرَكاؤُكُمُ الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 22], and His saying concerning them ﴿فَهَلْ لَنا مِن شُفَعاءَ فَيَشْفَعُوا لَنا﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 53], and other things that are numerous in the verses of the Qur'an.

[Page 140]

So His saying (lahu) is the predicate (khabar) of (laysa), because the genitive with the lām of exclusivity (lām al-ikhtiṣāṣ) is the focus of the predication, not the adverb of place. This is preferable to making (hāhunā) the predicate of (laysa) and making (lahu) an attribute of (ḥamīm), since there is no need for this attribution.

al-Ḥamīm is the close relative. Here it is a metonymy for the helper, since it is well known among the Arabs that a person's helpers are his clan and tribe.

﴿ولا طَعامٌ﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with (ḥamīm).

al-Ghislīn, with a kasra on the ghayn, is what enters the mouths of the people of the Fire of the flowing matters from the bodies, the water of the Fire, and the like, of what God knows. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 38–43:

﴿So I swear not by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ ﴿that this is indeed the word of a noble Messenger﴾ ﴿and it is not the word of a poet—little do you believe﴾ ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed﴾ ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The fa' (the "so" particle) here indicates a consequence (tafri') of the affirmation that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah and of the negation of what the polytheists attributed to it,

[Page 141]

as a consequence of what their denial of the Resurrection implied, namely an allusive (ta'ridh) denial of the Qur'an, which reported its occurrence, and their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), who said that it was revealed to him from Allah, the Exalted.

The discourse begins with an oath (qasam) to affirm its content, following the manner of oath-taking found in the Qur'an, and the discussion of it has already preceded at the words of the Exalted ﴿By those who line up in ranks﴾ [al-Saffat: 1].

The pronoun in (uqsimu) ("I swear") refers to Allah, the Exalted.

In this oath Allah gathered all the great things by which one is customarily sworn, from among the attributes of Allah the Exalted and from among His creatures that indicate the magnitude of His power. These two relative clauses, ﴿what you see﴾ and ﴿what you do not see﴾, encompass all of that. Among what they see are the earth, the mountains, the seas, human souls, the heavens and the stars. Among what they do not see are the spirits, the angels and the matters of the Hereafter.

The expression (la uqsimu) is a form that affirms an oath. Its original sense is abstention from swearing, the abstention of one who is scrupulous about swearing by the thing sworn by, out of fear of breaking the oath. Its use became widespread for every oath whose content one wishes to affirm. The particle (la) is treated as superfluous (mazid), as was mentioned previously at the words of the Exalted ﴿So I swear not by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75] in surah al-Waqi'ah. Some exegetes took the particle (la) in this oath to be a negation that cancels a preceding statement, and that the verb (uqsimu) after it is a resumed new sentence (isti'naf). This view has been refuted by the occurrence of its like at the beginnings of surahs, such as ﴿I swear not by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1] and ﴿I swear not by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1].

The pronoun in (innahu) ("indeed it") refers to the Qur'an, which is understood from the mention of the gathering and the Resurrection, for that is among what the Qur'an brought, and its bringing of that is among the greatest causes of their denial of it. Moreover, the use of the Qur'an as referent of the pronouns of absence (ghaybah) that have no antecedent mentioned has occurred repeatedly in it.

The emphasis of the statement by the particle (inna) and the lam is to refute those who denied that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah and attributed it to something else.

By "the noble Messenger" is meant Muhammad (ﷺ), as the conjunction of the Exalted's words ﴿And if he had attributed to Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44] requires. This is like the description of Musa (Moses) as ﴿a noble Messenger﴾ in the Exalted's words ﴿And We had certainly tried before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble Messenger﴾ [al-Dukhan: 17].

The attribution of (qawl, "word") to (rasul, "messenger") is because he is the one who conveyed it, so he is its speaker. The attribution is for the slightest connection; otherwise the Qur'an was made by Allah, the Exalted, and brought about upon the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ), just as it proceeded from Jibril (Gabriel) by His revelation through his mediation. The Exalted said ﴿We have only made it easy in your tongue﴾ [Maryam: 97].

[Page 142]

Muqatil narrated that the occasion of its revelation was that Abu Jahl said, "Muhammad is a poet," and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt said, "He is a soothsayer." So Allah the Exalted said ﴿Indeed it is the word of a noble Messenger﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse.

It is also possible that by ﴿a noble Messenger﴾ is meant Jibril (peace be upon him), as is meant in surah al-Takwir, since the apparent meaning there is Jibril, as will come.

In the word (rasul, "messenger") there is an indication that the speech is the speech of the one who sent it, that is, Allah the Exalted. This meaning has been emphasized by His words after it, ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾.
