The meaning is: you do not believe and you do not take heed, that is, at the time you say, "He is a poet," and "He is possessed," and no consideration is given to the belief of those among them who believed afterwards. The Exalted's words ﴿So few of them believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88] have preceded in surah al-Baqarah.

(Qalilan) is in the accusative in both places as an adjectival qualifier of an omitted verbal noun (masdar) that is indicated by (tu'minun, "you believe") and (tadhakkarun, "you take heed"). That is, you believe with a little belief, and you take heed with a little heeding.

The (ma) is an added particle for emphasis, like the words of Hatim al-Ta'i:

"Few are the heirs who will praise you for it, when he attains from what you were gathering some gain."

The two clauses ﴿little do you believe﴾ and ﴿little do you take heed﴾ are parenthetical (mu'taridhatan), meaning: the negation that it is the word of a poet has been established, and the negation that it is the word of a soothsayer has been established, and this negation does not secure your belief or your taking heed, because you are people of obstinacy.

Ibn Kathir, Hisham from Ibn 'Amir (the transmitters differed from Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir) and Ya'qub read both (tu'minun) and (tadhakkarun) with the feminine-second-person-plural form (taa' above, i.e. addressing "you"). The majority read both with the second-person form [as stated], while Ya'qub read them with the third-person yaa' below, as an iltifat (shift) from address to the third person. Their being parenthetical clauses makes this acceptable.

The negation of belief is placed on the side of the negation of their being the word of a poet, and the negation of taking heed on the side of the negation of their being the word of a soothsayer. This is because the negation that the Qur'an is the word of a poet is self-evident, since there is nothing in it resembling poetry, such as the balance of its parts in moving and still letters and the rhyme that is uniform in all the final segments. So their claim that it is the word of a poet is a deliberate slander that proclaims that their belief is not to be hoped for. As for the negation that the Qur'an is the word of a soothsayer, it requires slight reflection, since at first glance it may be confused for the listener, in that it is prose composed with closing rhymes (fawasil), and the speech of soothsayers is composed in paired rhymed prose (saj') of matching couplets. But when the listener reflects a little on its composition and its meanings, he knows that it is not the word of a soothsayer. Its composition differs from the composition of the soothsayers' speech, since its sections are not short and its closing rhymes are not in pairs with rhyme deliberately maintained, and its meanings are not among the meanings of soothsaying, which aims at reporting what will happen to some people of events, or the calamities expected to befall a people so that they may beware of them. Therefore the addressees of the verse are those from whom taking heed and reflection are negated. When this and that are both invalid, their claim is invalidated, and it is established that it is ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾, as the noble Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) claimed.

[Page 144]

The Exalted's words ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ are a second predicate of the subject of (inna), and it is an explicit statement after the metonymy.

You may make ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ the predicate of an omitted subject, whose omission follows the type that al-Sakkaki named "following usage" (mutaba'at al-istimal), which is frequent in eloquent speech, and make the clause a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because when the Qur'an was described as ﴿the word of a noble Messenger﴾ and negated from being the word of a poet or a soothsayer, the listener anticipated knowing its true nature, so it was explained that it is sent down from the Lord of the worlds upon the noble Messenger, so that he may say it to the people and recite it to them.

(Tanzil, "revelation") is a description by way of a verbal noun for intensification.

The meaning: indeed it is sent down from the Lord of the worlds upon the noble Messenger.

He expressed the Majesty by the description ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ rather than by His proper name, to alert that He is the Lord of the addressees and the Lord of the poets and soothsayers, who were held in esteem and admiration among them. This is like the words of Musa (Moses) to Pharaoh: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 26].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 44–47:

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings,﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand,﴾ ﴿then We would have cut from him the aorta,﴾ ﴿and not one of you could have withheld Us from him.﴾ This sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ [al-Haqqah: 38] ﴿and what you do not see﴾ [al-Haqqah: 39]. It is therefore included in what the particle fa' indicates of consequence, following from their denial of the Resurrection, which entailed their denial of the Qur'an and of the one who brought it, and their claim that it is a revelation from God, exalted is He.

The import of this sentence is a second argument that the Qur'an was sent down from God, in the manner of the theological method (al-madhhab al-kalami), following the first argument, which rested on the oath and the emphatic particles, in the manner of rhetorical argument (al-istidlal al-khitabi).

It is an argument from what is firmly established in minds: that God has perfect power and perfect knowledge, and so He would not permit anyone to attribute to Him a speech He did not utter. That is, if the Qur'an were not sent down from Us, and Muhammad claimed that it was sent down from Us, We would not have let him persist in that, and We would have hastened his destruction. The fact that he was not destroyed

[Page 145]

(ﷺ) indicates that he did not fabricate it against God, for (law) requires the negation of its condition's content because the negation of its consequent's content is established.

Two significant aims result from this discourse:

The first refers back to what preceded it: an additional refutation of the claim of the polytheists that the Qur'an is poetry or soothsaying, a refutation that comprehensively negates both kinds. That is, what clarifies the Qur'an's difference from these two kinds of speech is that the one who brings it attributes it to the revelation of God, and you know of no poet or soothsayer who claims that his speech is from God.

The second is the refutation of a claim of theirs that had not been explicitly refuted before: the statement of a group among them that he fabricated it, that is, that he attributed it to God falsely and invented it against God. God, exalted, said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Rather, they do not believe﴾ [al-Tur: 33]. So He made clear to them that if he had fabricated against God, He would not have let him persist in that.

Then this aim entails another aim: despairing them of his bringing a Qur'an that would not contradict their religion or ridicule their intellects and idols. God, exalted, said: (﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it."﴾ [Yunus: 15]). This sentence is coordinated as a parenthetical insertion (ʿaṭf iʿtiraḍ), so you may take the waw as parenthetical (iʿtiraḍiyya), for the waw of parenthesis has no meaning except this.

Al-taqawwul is attributing a saying to someone who did not say it. It is a form of tafaʿʿul from al-qawl, and it has this form, which indicates effort, because one who is attributed a saying by another that he did not say must make an effort and fabricate that speech. Because it is equivalent in meaning to lying, it is followed by ʿalā (against).

The meaning is: if he had lied against Us, reporting that We said a saying We did not say, and so on.

And (baʿḍa, "some") is a noun indicating a quantity of the kind of what it is added to. Here it is in the accusative as the direct object of taqawwala.

Al-aqawil is the plural of aqwal, which is itself the plural of qawl. That is, some of the kind of sayings, which are many; because of their number, a plural of a plural, which indicates abundance, was used for them. That is: even if he attributed to Us a small part of many true sayings, that is, if he attributed to Us a small portion of the Qur'an that We had not sent down, We would have seized him by the right hand, and so on to the end.

The meaning of ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ is: We would have seized him with power, that is, without delay. So the bāʾ is causal.

Al-yamin is the right hand. It is used metonymically for concern with control over what is seized, because the right hand is stronger in action than the left, owing to its frequent use; so attributing action to it is well known. This has been mentioned in several places, among them His saying ﴿And do not make God an obstacle for your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah: 224] in Surat al-Baqarah, His saying ﴿and from their right and from their left﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 17] in Surat al-Aʿraf, and His saying ﴿nor do you write it with your right hand﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 48] in Surat al-ʿAnkabut.

Abu al-Ghul al-Tahawi said:

"My soul and what my right hand possesses are ransom for horsemen who verified my suspicions concerning them."

The meaning is: We would have seized him swiftly, then We would have cut his aorta. In this there is an exaggeration of the image of the seizing, which is why it did not restrict itself to something like: "We would have destroyed him."

And (minhu, "from him") is connected to (akhadna, "seized") in the manner of an object to its verb. And (min) is redundant in affirmative speech according to the opinion of al-Akhfash and the Kufans, and this is the preferred view. I have explained this at His saying ﴿So We brought forth from it green [shoots], from which We bring forth grain piled up, and from the palm tree﴾ [al-Anʿam: 99], for (al-nakhl, "the palm tree") is coordinated with (khadiran, "green") with the addition of (min); and were it not for considering the redundancy, the grammar would not be sound except with difficulty. The benefit of the redundant (min) in speech is that its original function is partitive (al-tabʿid al-majazi) in an allusive manner, as if he were saying: We seize part of him.

Al-watin is a vessel to which the heart is attached, and it is called al-niyat. It is what supplies the body with blood, and for this reason it is called the river of the body. When it is cut, its owner dies, and it is cut at the slaughter of a camel.

So the cutting of the watin is among the conditions of the camel and its slaughter, and so the punishment of one who is supposed to have fabricated against God is likened to a camel that is slaughtered and whose watin is cut.

I have not found that the Arabs used a euphemism for destruction by cutting the watin, so this is one of the innovations of the Qur'an.

(Minhu, "from him") is either an attribute of al-watin, or connected to (qatʿna, "We cut"), that is, We removed it from him.

Between the first (minhu) and the second (minhu) there is an embellishment of paronomasia (jinas).

[Page 147]

As for the placement of the consequent clause ﴿So not one of you could have withheld Us from him﴾, it is closely connected to what the supposition of fabrication entailed of despairing them that he would fabricate against God a speech that would not displease them. In that situation of fabrication, if We seized him by the right hand and then cut his watin, not one of you or of others could withhold that punishment from him. Without this connection, the meaning of rendering them incapable of helping him would not appear, since they are not among those close enough to him in allegiance to be expected to help him. So the meaning of this verse revolves around the meaning of His saying: ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, to fabricate other than it against Us; and then they would have taken you as an intimate friend﴾ [al-Isra': 73]; ﴿And if We had not strengthened you, you would almost have inclined toward them a little﴾ [al-Isra': 74]; ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death; then you would not have found for yourself any helper against Us﴾ [al-Isra': 75].

The address in His saying (minkum, "of you") is to the polytheists.

He reported about (aḥad, "one") while it is singular, using the plural (ḥājizīn, "withholding"), because (aḥad) here, although its form is singular, has the meaning of the plural. For (aḥad), when it means a self or a person, occurs only in a context of negation, like (ʿarīb) and (dayyār) and similar indefinite nouns that are used only in negative contexts, and so it conveys generality: each one of you cannot withhold Us from him. The same form serves for the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. God, exalted, said: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], and He said: ﴿You are not like any of the women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32]. The meaning is: there are no people among you who can withhold Us from him.

Al-hajz is repelling and preventing. That is, not one of you can withhold Us from him. The pronoun refers to (rasulin karim, "a noble messenger").

The (min) in His saying (min aḥad) is redundant, for emphasis of the negation and for explicit indication of generality.

The mention of (minkum) together with (ʿanhu, "from him") is a deficient paronomasia (tajnis muharraf).

This verse is evidence that God, exalted, does not leave anyone who claims that God revealed to him a speech that he conveys to the people, and that He hastens his destruction.

As for one who claims prophethood without claiming a saying revealed to him, God may destroy him after a time, as was the case with al-Aswad al-ʿAnsi, who claimed prophethood in Yemen, and Musaylima al-Hanafi, who claimed prophethood in al-Yamama.

[Page 148]

Those two claimed prophethood but did not bring a speech that they attributed to God, exalted, so their destruction came after a period. Similar to them are those who claimed prophethood in Islam, such as (Babak and Mazyar).

Al-Fakhr said: It has been said: al-yamin means power and might, and the meaning is: We would have seized from him the yamin, that is, We would have removed power from him, and the bāʾ on this interpretation is an extra connective. Know that the sum of this is that if he had attributed to Us a saying We had not uttered, We would have restrained him from that, either by means of establishing proof, for We would have appointed for him one who would oppose him in it, and then it would have become clear to the people that he was lying in it, and that would be a refutation of his claim and a demolition of his speech; or by depriving him of the power to speak that saying, and this is what is required by the wisdom of God, exalted, so that the truthful is not confused with the liar. End quote. He constructed, from interpreting yamin as power, that the intended meaning is the power of the one who fabricates, not the power of God, and he derived from this an interpretation of the bāʾ as meaning an addition. None of the exegetes preceded him in this interpretation, and none after him followed him in it, as far as we have seen. There is room for scrutiny in it. What we have explained of the verse has shown that there is no need for al-Fakhr's interpretation.

Because it is equivalent in meaning to lying, it is followed by ʿalā (against).

The meaning is: if he had lied against Us, reporting that We said a saying We did not say, and so on.

And (baʿḍa, "some") is a noun indicating a quantity of the kind of what it is added to. Here it is in the accusative as the direct object of taqawwala.

Al-aqawil is the plural of aqwal, which is itself the plural of qawl. That is, some of the kind of sayings, which are many; because of their number, a plural of a plural, which indicates abundance, was used for them. That is: even if he attributed to Us a small part of many true sayings, that is, if he attributed to Us a small portion of the Qur'an that We had not sent down, We would have seized him by the right hand, and so on to the end.

The meaning of ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ is: We would have seized him with power, that is, without delay. So the bāʾ is causal.

Al-yamin is the right hand. It is used metonymically for concern with control over what is seized, because the right hand is stronger in action than the left, owing to its frequent use; so attributing action to it is well known. This has been mentioned in several places, among them His saying ﴿And do not make God an obstacle for your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah: 224] in Surat al-Baqarah, His saying ﴿and from their right and from their left﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 17] in Surat al-Aʿraf, and His saying ﴿nor do you write it with your right hand﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 48] in Surat al-ʿAnkabut.

Abu al-Ghul al-Tahawi said:

"My soul and what my right hand possesses are ransom for horsemen who verified my suspicions concerning them."

The meaning is: We would have seized him swiftly, then We would have cut his aorta. In this there is an exaggeration of the image of the seizing, which is why it did not restrict itself to something like: "We would have destroyed him."

And (minhu, "from him") is connected to (akhadna, "seized") in the manner of an object to its verb. And (min) is redundant in affirmative speech according to the opinion of al-Akhfash and the Kufans, and this is the preferred view. I have explained this at His saying ﴿So We brought forth from it green [shoots], from which We bring forth grain piled up, and from the palm tree﴾ [al-Anʿam: 99], for (al-nakhl, "the palm tree") is coordinated with (khadiran, "green") with the addition of (min); and were it not for considering the redundancy, the grammar would not be sound except with difficulty. The benefit of the redundant (min) in speech is that its original function is partitive (al-tabʿid al-majazi) in an allusive manner, as if he were saying: We seize part of him.

Al-watin is a vessel to which the heart is attached, and it is called al-niyat. It is what supplies the body with blood, and for this reason it is called the river of the body. When it is cut, its owner dies, and it is cut at the slaughter of a camel.

So the cutting of the watin is among the conditions of the camel and its slaughter, and so the punishment of one who is supposed to have fabricated against God is likened to a camel that is slaughtered and whose watin is cut.

I have not found that the Arabs used a euphemism for destruction by cutting the watin, so this is one of the innovations of the Qur'an.

(Minhu, "from him") is either an attribute of al-watin, or connected to (qatʿna, "We cut"), that is, We removed it from him.

Between the first (minhu) and the second (minhu) there is an embellishment of paronomasia (jinas).

[Page 147]

As for the placement of the consequent clause ﴿So not one of you could have withheld Us from him﴾, it is closely connected to what the supposition of fabrication entailed of despairing them that he would fabricate against God a speech that would not displease them. In that situation of fabrication, if We seized him by the right hand and then cut his watin, not one of you or of others could withhold that punishment from him. Without this connection, the meaning of rendering them incapable of helping him would not appear, since they are not among those close enough to him in allegiance to be expected to help him. So the meaning of this verse revolves around the meaning of His saying: ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, to fabricate other than it against Us; and then they would have taken you as an intimate friend﴾ [al-Isra': 73]; ﴿And if We had not strengthened you, you would almost have inclined toward them a little﴾ [al-Isra': 74]; ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death; then you would not have found for yourself any helper against Us﴾ [al-Isra': 75].

The address in His saying (minkum, "of you") is to the polytheists.

He reported about (aḥad, "one") while it is singular, using the plural (ḥājizīn, "withholding"), because (aḥad) here, although its form is singular, has the meaning of the plural. For (aḥad), when it means a self or a person, occurs only in a context of negation, like (ʿarīb) and (dayyār) and similar indefinite nouns that are used only in negative contexts, and so it conveys generality: each one of you cannot withhold Us from him. The same form serves for the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. God, exalted, said: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], and He said: ﴿You are not like any of the women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32]. The meaning is: there are no people among you who can withhold Us from him.

Al-hajz is repelling and preventing. That is, not one of you can withhold Us from him. The pronoun refers to (rasulin karim, "a noble messenger").

The (min) in His saying (min aḥad) is redundant, for emphasis of the negation and for explicit indication of generality.

The mention of (minkum) together with (ʿanhu, "from him") is a deficient paronomasia (tajnis muharraf).

This verse is evidence that God, exalted, does not leave anyone who claims that God revealed to him a speech that he conveys to the people, and that He hastens his destruction.

As for one who claims prophethood without claiming a saying revealed to him, God may destroy him after a time, as was the case with al-Aswad al-ʿAnsi, who claimed prophethood in Yemen, and Musaylima al-Hanafi, who claimed prophethood in al-Yamama.

[Page 148]

Those two claimed prophethood but did not bring a speech that they attributed to God, exalted, so their destruction came after a period. Similar to them are those who claimed prophethood in Islam, such as (Babak and Mazyar).

Al-Fakhr said: It has been said: al-yamin means power and might, and the meaning is: We would have seized from him the yamin, that is, We would have removed power from him, and the bāʾ on this interpretation is an extra connective. Know that the sum of this is that if he had attributed to Us a saying We had not uttered, We would have restrained him from that, either by means of establishing proof, for We would have appointed for him one who would oppose him in it, and then it would have become clear to the people that he was lying in it, and that would be a refutation of his claim and a demolition of his speech; or by depriving him of the power to speak that saying, and this is what is required by the wisdom of God, exalted, so that the truthful is not confused with the liar. End quote. He constructed, from interpreting yamin as power, that the intended meaning is the power of the one who fabricates, not the power of God, and he derived from this an interpretation of the bāʾ as meaning an addition. None of the exegetes preceded him in this interpretation, and none after him followed him in it, as far as we have seen. There is room for scrutiny in it. What we have explained of the verse has shown that there is no need for al-Fakhr's interpretation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verses 44–47:

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings,﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand,﴾ ﴿then We would have cut from him the aorta,﴾ ﴿and not one of you could have withheld Us from him.﴾ This sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ [al-Haqqah: 38] ﴿and what you do not see﴾ [al-Haqqah: 39]. It is therefore included in what the particle fa' indicates of consequence, following from their denial of the Resurrection, which entailed their denial of the Qur'an and of the one who brought it, and their claim that it is a revelation from God, exalted is He.

The import of this sentence is a second argument that the Qur'an was sent down from God, in the manner of the theological method (al-madhhab al-kalami), following the first argument, which rested on the oath and the emphatic particles, in the manner of rhetorical argument (al-istidlal al-khitabi).

It is an argument from what is firmly established in minds: that God has perfect power and perfect knowledge, and so He would not permit anyone to attribute to Him a speech He did not utter. That is, if the Qur'an were not sent down from Us, and Muhammad claimed that it was sent down from Us, We would not have let him persist in that, and We would have hastened his destruction. The fact that he was not destroyed

[Page 145]

(ﷺ) indicates that he did not fabricate it against God, for (law) requires the negation of its condition's content because the negation of its consequent's content is established.

Two significant aims result from this discourse:

The first refers back to what preceded it: an additional refutation of the claim of the polytheists that the Qur'an is poetry or soothsaying, a refutation that comprehensively negates both kinds. That is, what clarifies the Qur'an's difference from these two kinds of speech is that the one who brings it attributes it to the revelation of God, and you know of no poet or soothsayer who claims that his speech is from God.

God, exalted, said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Rather, they do not believe﴾ [al-Tur: 33]. So He made clear to them that if he had fabricated against God, He would not have let him persist in that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verse 48:

﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for those who fear Allah.﴾ It is conjoined to ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Haqqah: 40], and the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, whose pronoun was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Haqqah: 40]. When He nullified their slander against the Qur'an, that it is the speech of a poet or the speech of a soothsayer, He followed this with a statement of its nobility and benefit, to thoroughly refute their words by showing the clear distinction between it and the poetry of poets and the mumbling of soothsayers; for it is a reminder, and what they attached to it from the sayings of those people has no part in reminding at all.

Al-tadhkirah (tadhkirah, "reminder"): the verbal noun of tadhkir (reminding), which means alerting someone to what they have neglected.

The statement ﴿innahu tadhkirah﴾ ("it is a reminder") is a predication using the verbal noun for emphasis in the description. The meaning is that it reminds people of what they neglect of the knowledge of Allah and what befits His majesty, so that it may rescue them from the abyss of persisting in heedlessness until it is too late. Thus the Qur'an in itself is a reminder for whoever wishes to be mindful, whether or not he is mindful. The Qur'an has already been named "the Reminder" (al-dhikr) and "reminding" (al-tadhkir) in many verses, among them His saying, exalted is He, in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿Only as a reminder for one who fears﴾ [Ta-Ha: 3], and His saying ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed..."﴾ [al-Hijr: 6] in Surah al-Hijr.

By al-muttaqun (the God-fearing) is meant the believers, for they are the ones characterized by the fear of Allah, because they believe in resurrection and recompense, unlike the polytheists. The Qur'an was thus a guide for them to faith, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

Page 149
Whenever something of it was revealed, or they recited some of it, it reminded them of what they already knew, lest heedlessness or forgetfulness overtake them. Thus the Qur'an is a reminder for the God-fearing in the past, the present and the future, for the predication of it by the name of the verbal noun bears all three tenses, since the verbal noun carries no indication of time, unlike the verb and what resembles it.

The phrase ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾ ("for the God-fearing") is attached to its being a reminder because the God-fearing are the ones who perceived its excellence.

﴿And indeed We know that among you are deniers﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a source of regret for the disbelievers﴾. These are two related sentences. The first serves as a preface and introduction to the second, and it is interposed between the sentence before it and the one after it. The second of them is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Haqqah: 48]. Placing the first sentence before the second was intended to draw the attention of the deniers to their own condition. It also served as a completion (tatmim) of the sentence ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Haqqah: 48].

The meaning is: We sent the Messenger to you with this Qur'an, while We know that among you there will be those who deny him and it. Our knowledge of that did not turn Us away from directing the admonition to you and repeating it to you, so that whoever perishes may perish with a clear proof, and whoever lives may live with a clear proof. Thus the attribute of the Qur'an that benefits the God-conscious was contrasted with its attribute that harms the disbelievers, in the manner of opposition (tadadd). Between the two conjoined sentences there is therefore the embellishment of antithesis (tibaq).

The hasrah (regret) is intense and repeated remorse over a lost thing that is desired. It is also called talahhuf. It is derived from al-hasr, which means uncovering, because its cause is uncovered for the one who experiences it after the opportunity to grasp it has passed, and it keeps recurring to him. So "the Qur'an is a source of regret for the disbelievers" means that it is a cause of regret for them in this world and in the next. It is a regret for them in this world because it exposed their falsehoods, undermined the pillar of their false religion, and uncovered the baseness of their idols. It is a regret for them in the next world because they will find that opposing it is the cause of their punishment, and they will come to certain knowledge that what it called them to was the means of success had they followed it, especially since they will have seen the good end of those who believed in it.

The deniers (al-mukadhdhibun) are the disbelievers. The shift from a pronoun referring to them to the explicit noun was made because the regret encompasses the deniers of that day and those who will disbelieve in it later.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 69, verse 51:

Page 150
﴿And indeed, it is the truth of certainty﴾ is coordinated with ﴿And indeed, it is a regret for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Haqqah: 50]. It is possible that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, since these are among the attributes of the Qur'an. It is also possible that what is meant by it is the thing mentioned, namely that the Qur'an is a regret for the disbelievers; that is, that this is undoubtedly true, meaning that it brings about their regret in this world or in the Hereafter.

The annexation of "truth" (haqq) to "certainty" (yaqin) may be an annexation of the qualified to the qualifier, meaning: it is the true certainty, described as a certainty about which no one doubts its being true except one whose insight has been veiled. This is preferable to making the annexation one of the qualifier to the qualified, meaning "for the true certainty," that is, the certainty which no doubt afflicts.

Know that "ḥaqq al-yaqīn" (truth of certainty), "ʿayn al-yaqīn" (eye of certainty), and "ʿilm al-yaqīn" (knowledge of certainty) all occur in the Qur'an.

"Ḥaqq al-yaqīn" occurs in this surah and at the end of Surah al-Waqi'ah. "ʿIlm al-yaqīn" and "ʿayn al-yaqīn" occur in Surah al-Takathur. These three compounds, their annexation is, as we have mentioned, either of the qualifier to the qualified or of the qualified to the qualifier. The meaning of each compound is the sum of what its two words and their annexation indicate.

The scholars have settled on making the phrase "ʿilm al-yaqīn" a technical term for what evidence gives by conceiving matters as they really are, according to the words of al-Sayyid al-Jurjani in his book al-Ta'rifat (Definitions). In the words of Abu al-Baqa' in al-Kulliyyat there occurs what indicates that some of these compounds were transferred into certain scientific technical terminologies and became titles for meanings. He said: "ʿIlm al-yaqīn" is for the people of demonstration, while "ʿayn al-yaqīn" and "ḥaqq al-yaqīn" are also for the people of unveiling and direct vision, such as the prophets and the saints, according to their differing degrees. He said: The investigating philosophers have established that after the four levels of the soul's acquisition of knowledge, mentioned in logic—the self-evident truths, the inner observations, the experiments, and the widely transmitted reports—there are two levels:

The first is the level of ʿayn al-yaqīn, which is that the soul becomes such that it witnesses the intelligibles in the knowledges that the soul emanates, as they are. The second is the level of ḥaqq al-yaqīn, which is that the soul becomes such that it connects with the intelligibles by an intellectual connection and meets its own essence with a spiritual meeting. The scholars of Sufism settled on making each compound of these three a title for a meaning of intellectual unveiling, and they occur in the book al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya of Shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn 'Arabi.

[Page 152]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (al-basmala)
Surat al-Ma'arij

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent.﴾ This is a consequence of everything that preceded it: the description of the Qur'an, its exoneration from the slanders, the exoneration of the Prophet (ﷺ) from what the polytheists had fabricated against him, and what God strengthened him with, namely the citing of the examples of the peoples who denied the messengers to those who denied the Qur'an. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to glorify God with glorification of praise and exaltation, in gratitude to Him for the blessing He had bestowed upon him: the blessing of prophethood and the sending down of this Qur'an to him.

"The name of God" is the proper name that denotes the Essence.

The "bi" (ba') here denotes accompaniment, meaning: glorify God with speech, glorifying Him. This is because it combines belief in His transcendence, affirmation of it, and making it widely known.

Tasbih (glorification) is declaring God free from deficiencies through belief, worship and speech. Therefore, in verbal glorification it was necessary that the name of the one being glorified be used, which is why He said ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord﴾ and did not say "So glorify your Lord, the Magnificent." The reason for inserting a noun in His saying "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" has already been explained in the discussion of the basmala.

Glorifying the Benefactor through belief and speech is the attainable extent of the gratitude of the grateful, since they cannot reach His thanks by anything beyond that. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Included in this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) continuance in discharging his message and conveying it." It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when this verse was revealed, said: "Make it part of your bowing (ruku')." A group of scholars recommended adhering to this, while Malik disliked adhering to it lest it be regarded as obligatory and binding." End of quote.

A parallel to this verse has preceded, at the end of Surat al-Waqi'a.

The Surah is named in the books of Sunnah, in Sahih al-Bukhari and Jami' al-Tirmidhi, and in the tafsirs of al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir, as "Surat Sa'ala Sa'il" (the Surah "A Questioner Asked"). Likewise, I have seen it in some manuscript Qur'ans in Kufic script in Qayrawan in the fifth century.

In most eastern and western Qur'an manuscripts and in most tafsirs, it is named "Surat al-Ma'arij" (the Surah of the Ascending Stairways). The Itqan mentions that it is also called "Surat al-Waqi'" (the Surah of the Inevitable Event).

These three names are derived from words that occur at its beginning. The one most specifically associated with it is the phrase "Sa'ala sa'il," because a similar phrase does not occur in any other Surah of the Qur'an. However, the name "Surat al-Ma'arij" came to predominate because it is lighter.

It is Meccan by consensus. Someone who said that the verse ﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾ (al-Ma'arij 70:24) is Medinan is an outlier.

[Page 153 continued]
It is the seventy-eighth Surah in the order of revelation of the Surahs of the Qur'an. According to Jabir ibn Zayd, it was revealed after Surat al-Haqqa and before Surat al-Naba'.

The majority of regional scholars counted its verses as forty-four. The people of Syria counted them as forty-three.

* * *

Its purposes:
It contains, among its themes, a warning to the disbelievers of the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, affirmation of that Day, and description of its terrors.

It describes something of God's majesty in it, and the terrifying nature of the abode of punishment, which is Hell, and mentions the causes that make one deserving of its punishment.

It contrasts this with the deeds of the believers that earned them the abode of honor, which are the opposites of the attributes of the disbelievers.

It affirms and steadies the Prophet (ﷺ), and consoles him for what he encounters from the polytheists.

It describes many of the qualities of the Muslims that Islam instilled in them, and warns the polytheists against their extermination and their replacement by people better than them.
